title: Study on the interaction between epicatechin gallate and bovine myosin and its enhancement of protein structure and function.
authors: Zheng, Wentao; Wan, Xiaohui; Zhang, Duoduo; Ding, Jiwei; Ma, Bohan; Shu, Qin; Liu, Yongfeng
abstract: Bovine myosin is a critical protein influencing meat product quality, yet its conformation is susceptible to destabilization during processing. This study investigated the interaction mechanism between epicatechin gallate (ECG) and bovine myosin, as well as its regulatory effects on protein structure and functional properties. Spectroscopic analyses revealed that ECG bound to myosin through static quenching, altering the microenvironment of aromatic amino acid residues. FTIR further showed that ECG induced protein secondary structure rearrangement and promoted the formation of beta-sheet structure. Molecular simulation revealed that hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions were the dominant forces for stabilizing ECG-myosin binding. Glu331, Ile326 and Asp242 were identified as the key residues for the stable binding of the complex. Interestingly, at an ECG concentration of 100 mumol/L, the polyphenol binding rate reached 25.76%, DPPH radical scavenging capacity increased by approximately 5.2-fold, surface hydrophobicity markedly decreased, and solubility was enhanced by nearly 6-fold. In vitro digestion experiments showed that ECG delayed protein hydrolysis in the gastric phase but promoted both protein digestion and polyphenol release in the intestinal phase. Collectively, ECG significantly improved the physicochemical and functional properties of bovine myosin, and providing a scientific basis for the application of tea polyphenols in meat protein systems.

title: Functional characterization of PfHDDCP reveals a HotDog-domain acyl‑CoA thioesterase as a potential antimalarial drug target.
authors: Gupta, Pooja; Kaushik, Naveen Kumar; Goyal, Parveen; Dhir, Sunny; Pai, Somnath S; Sharma, Anil
abstract: BACKGROUND: Thioesterases play a central role in maintaining acyl‑CoA homeostasis and lipid metabolic flux, processes that are critical for the intraerythrocytic development of Plasmodium falciparum. Plasmodium falciparum HotDog domain-containing protein [PfHDDCP (PF3D7_1135400; previously annotated as PF11_0364, XP_001348035.1)] has been computationally predicted to function as an acyl-CoA thioesterase, although experimental validation was lacking. Here, we present the first biochemical characterization of PfHDDCP and demonstrate its thioesterase activity. METHODS AND RESULTS: The PfHDDCP gene was cloned into the pRSET-A vector, expressed in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3), purified under denaturing conditions, and refolded. Enzymatic assays revealed no detectable protease activity but demonstrated robust thioesterase activity toward acetyl-CoA using a DTNB-based colorimetric assay. Kinetic analysis yielded a Km of 11.68 microM and a Vmax of 16.28 x 10(-)(5) micromol/min, with substrate inhibition at elevated acetyl-CoA concentrations. PfHDDCP showed maximal catalytic activity at pH 8.0 and 37  degrees C and retained substantial activity at 40-42  degrees C. Fe(2)(+) and Ca(2)(+) had no significant effect on activity, whereas Mg(2)(+) markedly reduced activity at the higher concentrations tested. Molecular docking predicted favorable heme binding, but neither spectroscopy nor native PAGE supported stable heme association in vitro. Artemisinin derivatives showed favorable predicted interactions with PfHDDCP and inhibited its thioesterase activity in vitro, whereas chloroquine had a substantially weaker effect. CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings establish PfHDDCP as a functional HotDog domain-containing acyl-CoA thioesterase and support its potential involvement in parasite lipid metabolism. The inhibition observed with selected antimalarial compounds identifies PfHDDCP as a candidate for further investigation of drug-enzyme interactions. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not Applicable.

title: Comparative Hydrophobicity Analysis of Human beta-Tubulin and Bacterial FtsZ Using the Fuzzy Oil Drop Model: Potential Implications for Chaperone-Assisted Folding.
authors: Roterman, Irena; Stapor, Katarzyna; Dulak, Dawid; Konieczny, Leszek
abstract: The issue of protein folding in vivo remains an unsolved problem despite important progress achieved by artificial intelligence (AlphaFold). Experimental studies have shown that there are several mechanisms involved in this process. The main distinction concerns the involvement of chaperone proteins in this process as opposed to spontaneous folding. Evolutionary analysis shows that tubulin in eukaryotic organisms requires engagement of the ATP-dependent ring-shaped chaperonin TRiC/CCT, while the homologous protein in prokaryotic organisms obtains its functional structure without the support from other proteins. This study-limited to 2 examples: one human tubulin beta chain and one structure of homologous bacterial FtsZ protein-presents hypothetical interpretation of these differences based on the external conditions for folding process. The differences of the distribution of hydrophobicity in the compared proteins are taken as the criteria for comparison. The fuzzy oil drop model (FOD-M) assumes the folding of prokaryotic proteins as a spontaneous process aided only by the presence of the water environment that directs the folding toward the generation of a centrally located hydrophobic core with a polar surface. Eukaryotic protein-tubulin-exhibits a distribution of hydrophobicity that lacks this type of order as it is interpreted based on the FOD-M assumptions. The difference seems to be the result of the involvement of different external force fields in the folding process. These 2 proteins are an example that suggest the need to include the active influence of the local environment. The hypothesis for in silico methods of folding process simulation is assumed to use a multiple-object optimization technique that takes into account the optimization of the energy state of protein E as a function dependent on 2 functions: E (INT) (internal force field) and E (EXT) (external force field).

title: MultiTargetDB: a comprehensive database of multitarget ligands for polypharmacology research and drug discovery.
authors: Pan, Jinmei; Lin, Haoyu; Zhu, Jintao; Xie, Weixin; Li, Yu; Xie, Jin; Zhang, Shuaipeng; Hong, Liangli; Lai, Luhua; Pei, Jianfeng; Dong, Geng
abstract: Multitarget drug discovery has gained considerable traction in recent years, particularly for the treatment of complex diseases. Despite the growing demand for dedicated, well-curated resources to advance polypharmacology research and rational multitarget drug discovery, such resources remain severely limited. Here, we present MultiTargetDB, a database of multitarget ligands integrated with comprehensive biological annotations and measurement-level provenance. At the small molecule level, MultiTargetDB integrates chemical structures (including molecular scaffolds), their drug development stages, and target information, whereas at the target level, MultiTargetDB incorporates protein domains and families, functional associations, and pathway-disease annotations. The current release contains 173 977 multitarget molecules, 6496 protein targets, and 474 749 standardized quantitative bioactivity records, complemented by 46 234 high-confidence protein functional associations, 370 pathways from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and 2493 diseases. MultiTargetDB supports multitarget ligand retrieval, target-combination analysis, quantitative activity profiling, inspection of source-level evidence, and biological interpretation of molecule-target-pathway-disease relationships, with a natural-language query assistant facilitating flexible database exploration. The integrated quantitative, pharmacological and biological data further provide a basis for drug-repurposing exploration, computational modeling, and machine-learning applications. MultiTargetDB v1.0 is freely accessible at https://multitargetdb.inflygent.com/.

title: Host genomic context determines the direction of an oracle-predicted sequence effect: a composition-preserving CpG intervention in Enformer and Borzoi.
authors: Uysal, Selahattin Alperen
abstract: Sequence-to-function models are increasingly used as oracles to score designed regulatory elements, on the untested assumption that an effect measured at one locus holds at another. Taking chromatin and host loci from multiple sclerosis risk regions, we kept four questions apart: sequence realism, transfer of discrimination, edit stability, calibration. A sixth-order Markov chain reproduced the cell-type-specific motif enrichment a trained transformer missed, despite its lower held-out likelihood. Scores differ in level between loci far more than between inserts at one locus, yet inserts selected by an Enformer-derived index kept 85% of their advantage at four unseen loci. Once GC was matched, however, the index separated peak-derived from inaccessible sequence at none of 12 hosts, and from random sequence in opposite directions at different hosts. Placing identical inserts and an identical CpG edit at 24 host loci, the effect varied far beyond sampling noise on host identity alone ([Formula: see text]), unpredicted by 18 host properties. It survives scoring only the bins the insert occupies ([Formula: see text], and across 200 loci), so is no artefact of aggregation; the apparent host dominance, however, falls from 25-fold to 3-fold under that localised score, and the one locus positive under the whole-window score reverses under it. Borzoi reproduced the heterogeneity but not its amplitude, and the objective did not predict lentiMPRA activity. For these two oracles and this edit, the size of a predicted effect depends on where it is measured, and its direction at any one locus is not robust.

title: Codon optimization as a design variable in biotherapeutics.
authors: Jankowska, Katarzyna I; Katneni, Upendra K; Stauft, Charles B; Kimchi-Sarfaty, Chava
abstract: Codon optimization (CO) is a key design variable in biotherapeutics that is used to enhance expression of recombinant proteins, gene therapies, and vaccines. Although synonymous codon substitutions were historically considered neutral, codon choice can influence messenger RNA (mRNA) stability, translation kinetics, cotranslational folding, and immunogenicity. Current optimization strategies integrate computational parameters including codon adaptation indices, tRNA availability, mRNA structure, cytosine-phosphate-guanine dinucleotide content, codon pair bias, and machine learning approaches to balance expression and product quality. Additionally, dynamic tRNA modifications within the epitranscriptome modulate codon-biased translation in a context-dependent manner. While CO has not been implicated in adverse clinical outcomes, its context-dependent effects on protein conformation, post-translational modifications, and immune responses necessitate rigorous characterization. This opinion article presents our viewpoint on mechanisms, applications, and regulatory considerations for CO in biologics.

title: Dynamic structural adaptation of a conserved interaction hotspot in the respiratory syncytial virus fusion glycoprotein F.
authors: Kaushik, Rahul; Re, Suyong
abstract: Protein interaction sites must maintain structural integrity while accommodating conformational fluctuations and sequence perturbations. Molecular determinants that distinguish locally adaptable residues from structurally constrained positions within conserved interfaces remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigate this problem using the prefusion respiratory syncytial virus fusion glycoprotein F as a model system, focusing on a conserved interaction hotspot proximal to the MEDI8897-binding interface. An integrated computational framework combining evolutionary conservation, structure-based energetic analysis, residue interaction networks, and molecular dynamics simulations was used to characterize mutation-dependent structural responses. Analysis of 1848 RSV F sequences revealed strong conservation of the CPINKC hotspot comprising C69, P205, I206, N208, K209, and C212. Despite conservation, saturation mutagenesis and structural analysis revealed pronounced heterogeneity in calculated energetic response to substitution. P205R and N208R produced highly unfavorable calculated energetic effects, whereas I206R exhibited an approximately neutral energetic response. Residue interaction network analysis identified I206 as topologically central residue with the highest betweenness and closeness centrality within the hotspot. Aggregate MD sampling comprised three independent 500-ns simulations for each of seven systems, yielding 10.5 mus of total simulation time. All systems retained the overall prefusion architecture over the simulated timescale but exhibited distinct local and interprotomer responses. N208R produced the strongest local perturbation, including increased hotspot flexibility and reduced interprotomer contact occupancy. In contrast, P205R maintained restrained local dynamics despite its energetic penalty, whereas I206R preserved a broadly wild-type-like dynamic profile. These findings indicate that energetic cost, residue interaction topology, and conformational dynamics provide complementary information for characterizing mutation-induced structural adaptation.

title: ERIS2: A deep-learning platform for predicting mutation-induced protein stability changes.
authors: Ekambaram, Srinivasan; Kundu, Debarshi; Ghosh, Swaroop; Dokholyan, Nikolay V
abstract: Accurately predicting changes in protein thermodynamic stability upon mutation is a fundamental challenge in protein engineering and therapeutics. Deep learning has improved prediction, but many models remain limited by small, imbalanced training data and poor generalization across mutation types. Here, we present ERIS2, an attention-convolutional deep learning framework that integrates contextual sequence embeddings with atomistic and residue-level structural features from experimental protein structures to predict mutation-induced stability changes. Trained on large-scale experimental measurements combined with curated ProTherm data, a 5-fold ERIS2 ensemble achieved Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.69 on S461, 0.51 on S669, and 0.60 on S96, three blind-test datasets sequence-disjoint from all training configurations, and showed negligible anti-symmetry bias on Ssym forward and reverse pairs. ERIS2 is freely available as a structure-based web server without registration, providing a robust framework for protein stability prediction and advancing computational tools for protein engineering and therapeutic design.

title: Sequence Scanning Improves Accuracy for Antibody-Antigen and Molecular Glue Ternary Complex Cofolding.
authors: Linker, Stephanie M; Ploetz, Tobias; Evers, Andreas; Musil, Djordje; Kaiser, Jesko; Schindler, Christina
abstract: Accurately modeling biomolecular interactions is crucial for understanding biological function and can accelerate drug discovery efforts. Deep-learning-based cofolding methods such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 can successfully predict many different biomolecular complexes. However, these models show lower success rates in predicting antibody-antigen and molecular glue (MG) ternary complexes, two cases of high relevance to pharmaceutical research. Here, we present sequence scanning, a new workflow, evaluated on Boltz and Protenix, that improves prediction accuracy in these domains by applying systematic constraints to enhance overall sampling diversity. For both use cases, we assess the performance of the method on large, diverse benchmark sets. We find improved accuracy of the sequence scanning workflow in predicting antibody-antigen interface contacts and in pose prediction quality for MGs compared to previously published results. We also discuss remaining challenges and potential improvements to the method.

title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase.
authors: Aparicio, David; Ortigosa, Juan R; Guay, Kevin P; Williams, Robert V; Lannot, Jorge O; Zong, Guanghui; Comino, Natalia; Rodriguez, Jose F; Wang, Lai-Xi; Marti, Marcelo A; Roversi, Pietro; Hebert, Daniel N; Gierasch, Lila M; Modenutti, Carlos P; Guerin, Marcelo E
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to "open" and "closed" architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase.
authors: Guenon, Paul; Chauveau, Marion; Filipowska, Karolina; Tunon, Inaki; Nizak, Clement; Reynolds, Kimberly A; Stirnemann, Guillaume; Rivoire, Olivier; Laage, Damien
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

title: RNA Tertiary Structure Prediction and Analysis Using NuFold and the NuFold Database.
authors: Liu, Boyuan; Kagaya, Yuki; Platt, David; Kihara, Daisuke
abstract: Accurate prediction of RNA tertiary structure is critical for understanding the functions of diverse non-coding RNAs, yet experimental structure determination remains challenging and resource intensive. Inspired by advances in deep learning for protein structure prediction, NuFold was developed as an end-to-end framework that predicts all-atom RNA tertiary structures directly from sequence. NuFold integrates evolutionary information from multiple sequence alignments and predicted secondary structure features to construct 3D coordinates of RNA. To maximize accessibility, NuFold is available as open-source software, supported by a Google Colab notebook for browser-based prediction and NuFold DB, a large-scale repository of precomputed RNA structures. This chapter provides a practical guide to using these resources, enabling researchers to generate and interpret RNA structural models without extensive computational resources, and thereby facilitating structural and functional studies in RNA biology.

title: Meta-Scoring Approach to Curate Synthetic RNA 3D Structures.
authors: Bernard, Clement; Justyna, Marek; Postic, Guillaume; Antczak, Maciej; Tahi, Fariza; Szachniuk, Marta
abstract: The structural diversity of RNA is central to molecular medicine, RNA-targeted drug discovery, and synthetic biology, where engineered RNA molecules are increasingly used in therapeutic, regulatory, and nanotechnology applications. While the rapid development of deep learning methods has heightened the demand for large, diverse structural datasets, high-quality RNA data remain scarce compared to protein datasets. Synthetic RNA structure datasets can help address this gap by enabling large-scale exploration of conformational space; however, their practical utility depends on careful curation and validation to ensure reliability. Here, we present a pipeline, RNA-SyntHub, for systematically constructing curated synthetic RNA datasets. The workflow integrates data from multiple structure-generation approaches with a meta-scoring function to identify low-quality models and select high-confidence candidates. As a proof of concept, we applied this method to a dataset of 447,402 synthetic RNA structures predicted by RFDiffusion, obtaining a curated subset of approximately 16,000 structures, further complemented with predictions from Boltz-1 and RNAComposer. This study provides both a methodological framework for generating and curating large collections of synthetic RNA 3D models under explicitly stated assumptions and a concrete dataset that supports methodological development, exploratory analyses, decoy-based applications, and selected deep learning workflows in RNA design, synthetic biology, and nanotechnology.

title: Fine-Tuning a Protein Language Model for Epitope Library Generation and Sequence Filtering.
authors: Flechas Manrique, Natalia; Martinez Diez, Alberto; Lopez-Martinez, Elena; Andrea, Luc; Cortajarena, Aitziber L; Espinosa-Portales, Llorenc; Manteca, Aitor
abstract: Linear peptide epitopes play a key role in vaccines, immunotherapies, and diagnostics, yet discovering them remains difficult because peptide sequence space grows exponentially and experimentally confirmed epitopes are relatively few. This chapter presents a computational framework for the generation of synthetic linear epitope libraries that reproduce key statistical and sequence-level properties of naturally occurring epitopes. A large language model pre-trained on protein sequences and subsequently fine-tuned on curated epitope datasets is employed to generate biologically plausible peptide candidates beyond those observed experimentally. To further enrich functional relevance of the generated sequences, they are filtered using transformer-based classification models trained on viral and bacterial epitope datasets. These models are applied as discriminative tools to distinguish likely epitopes from non-epitopes rather than to infer pathogen origin. The resulting libraries are designed to be compatible with high-throughput experimental screening platforms, such as droplet microfluidics, enabling efficient integration of generative artificial intelligence with experimental immunology workflows.

title: TRAILS-MD: Mapping complex conformational landscapes and transition pathways via lightweight lineage-aware adaptive sampling.
authors: Maity, Dibyendu; Majumdar, Rupak; Chakrabarty, Suman
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are fundamentally limited by the timescale gap between rapid atomic fluctuations and slow, activated conformational transitions. While adaptive sampling accelerates the exploration of metastable states, conventional implementations often obscure the dynamical connectivity between discovered basins, confusing broad configurational coverage with the sampling of physically viable transition pathways. Here, we present a lightweight, engine-agnostic adaptive sampling framework (TRAILS-MD) that iteratively launches short trajectory ensembles across either fixed or on-the-fly machine-learned (ML) collective-variable (CV) spaces. A defining feature of our approach is explicit trajectory lineage preservation, which allows for the rigorous reconstruction of connected pathways from highly parallelized, disjointed exploration stages. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework across a hierarchy of molecular challenges: overcoming low-dimensional barriers in peptide isomerization, navigating entropic bottlenecks in protein folding (Trp-cage and WW domain), mapping transient exit tunnels during ligand unbinding (HSP90), and exploring large conformational changes in adenylate kinase. Finally, we show how lineage-aware exploratory ensembles can seamlessly seed unbiased production trajectories for the construction of Markov state models (MSMs). By bridging the gap between deep-learning-driven coordinate discovery and strict parent-child trajectory tracking, this framework democratizes advanced data-driven sampling for routine computational biophysics workflows.

title: Beyond Static Structures: New Opportunities to Model the Dynamic Interactions of Cell-Surface Proteins.
authors: Wu, Yinghao
journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology
abstract: Recent advances in AI-driven structure prediction have transformed structural biology but remain limited for cell-surface proteins mediating transient, context-dependent interactions. Multidomain architectures, flexible linkers, and coupled cis- and trans-interactions challenge current models, leading to inaccurate predictions for key adhesion molecules. These limitations highlight the need to incorporate cellular context, conformational dynamics, and multivalent interactions. Emerging strategies, including MD-informed machine learning, generative models, and multiscale simulations integrated with experimental restraints, offer promising solutions. Together, these approaches aim to bridge static structure prediction with dynamic, physiologically relevant modeling of protein interactions at cell-cell interfaces.

title: SVEP1 enables efficient binding of angiopoietin-2 to the TIE1 receptor, allowing receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling.
authors: Uphoff, Katharina; Hussmann, Melina; Peters, Oliver; Morgelin, Matthias; Metzen, Fabian; Obermann, Wolfgang M J; Bazan, Fernando J; Stetefeld, Jorg; Koch, Manuel; Schulte-Merker, Stefan; Schulte-Ostermann, Dorte
abstract: The molecular mechanisms that drive (lymph-)angiogenesis are crucial to understanding diseases, such as lymphedema, that are caused due to malformations of the lymphatic vasculature. Recently, an interaction between the secreted protein Svep1, a key regulator in lymphangiogenesis, and the transmembrane receptor Tie1 was shown in zebrafish, humans, and mice. Here, guided by in silico AlphaFold-multimer structure predictions of SVEP1 complexes, we assert with protein binding studies that the human CCP20 domain is the primary binding site for TIE1. We further demonstrate that SVEP1 mediates strong binding of ANG2 and TIE1, and that combined stimulation of hdLECs with SVEP1 and ANG2 leads to phosphorylation of TIE1. TIE1 activation by SVEP1 and ANG2 enables downstream signaling and, in turn, potentiates nuclear exclusion of FOXO1 and phosphorylation of AKT compared to SVEP1 or ANG2 alone. We present a model in which ANG1/2 dimers bind to both SVEP1 and TIE1, resulting in the recruitment of multiple TIE1 receptor molecules to a multimeric complex at the cell membrane, potentially amplifying its signaling capacity.

title: Aptamers without SELEX: De novo design from protein structure in hours.
authors: Dolgusheva, Vladislava A; Leibin, Iosif V; Kudryashova, Natalia O; Mukanov, Artem R; Kuznetsov, Ivan I; Manasyan, Artem L; Pavlyuk, Gleb A; Mishkorez, Ivan V; Keremet, Anna M; Podlesnyi, Pavel R; Kalinkin, Alexey N; Avdeev, Kirill S; Kuznetsov, Maxim D; Parfenov, Nikita O; Gromov, Stanislav M; Ufaev, Dmitry; Nasaev, Shamsudin S
abstract: Systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX)-based aptamer discovery can be constrained by target availability, selection biases, and optimization requirements. We introduce Xelari, a modular pipeline for de novo DNA and RNA aptamer design from protein structures without target-specific SELEX data or retraining. Xelari combines algorithmic modules with surrogate models trained on physical or structural references. InNA reproduced nucleotide-amino-acid interaction energies with RMSE of 0.19 kcal/mol across 483,735 reference pairs. AliNA achieved a mean F1 of 0.757 on 339 PDB-derived RNA evaluation sequences. Edgar correlated with experimental folding energies but did not reproduce their absolute scale, supporting its use as a ranking heuristic. Under the reported calibration, ValentiNA showed MAE of 0.931 kcal/mol and Spearman rho of 0.795 across 32 retrospective records associated with 27 structural templates; this analysis does not establish family-independent validation. Prospectively, three DNA aptamers designed against Treponema pallidum protein structures showed cell-associated binding in a treponeme assay (apparent K(D), 0.91-2.57 muM). A fourth DNA aptamer served as a capture reagent in a serum-based hybrid aptamer-antibody assay for Tau441. These applications support feasibility without establishing intended-target engagement in the cellular assay or a general success rate, positioning structure-based design as a complement to experimental selection.

title: Simulating Directed Evolution In Silico with an Iterative, Physics-Based Workflow.
authors: Jones, Chey M; Verma, Deeptak
abstract: Directed evolution consistently delivers engineered enzymes that facilitate diverse biocatalytic transformations. Despite advances in automation and high-throughput workflows, our ability to rapidly engineer novel enzymes is limited by our inability to thoroughly sample the vast protein design space. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) methods have alleviated this challenge to some degree, due to their ability to propose mutations based on learned patterns from complex protein data sets. However, the hidden logic of these AI-based methods can complicate our ability to reveal and exploit fundamental details of these enzymes. To complement these hidden-logic models, we present a structure- and physics-based workflow that mimics directed evolution in silico. This Virtual Protein EngineeR (referred to as ViPER) aims to simulate directed evolution by leveraging computational modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, in silico mutagenesis, and structure-based property evaluation to iteratively engineer an enzyme toward a desired target. In this work, we present a retrospective analysis to demonstrate ViPER's ability to efficiently navigate the complex protein-protein interfaces associated with the oligomerization of a ketoreductase (KRED) enzyme. In addition to successfully predicting >70% of sites that are crucial for toggling the oligomerization of this KRED enzyme (after only five rounds), this dynamics-based methodology identifies a distal mutation that was incorporated during experiment-based directed evolution. This work provides a novel foundation for computationally driven directed evolution efforts, opening the opportunity to simultaneously pursue and evaluate multiple evolutionary routes through a physics-based lens.

title: Deep Learning for Protein Secondary-Structure Segmentation in Intermediate-Resolution Cryo-EM Maps: A Resolution-Stratified Benchmark Dataset and Controlled Evaluation.
authors: Pial, Md Ehashan Rabbi; Dehan, Farhan Noor; Sazzed, Salim
abstract: Accurate segmentation of protein secondary structures in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps is crucial for protein tracing and atomic model building, yet remains challenging at intermediate resolutions. Although deep learning architectures have recently been applied to this task, there remains a lack of standardized evaluation protocols and systematic resolution-stratified analyses. Consequently, it remains unclear how segmentation performance varies across finer resolution ranges within the intermediate-resolution regime and how different volumetric segmentation architectures compare under controlled experimental conditions. To address these gaps, we present a nonredundant, resolution-stratified benchmark dataset and a controlled evaluation framework for protein secondary-structure segmentation in intermediate-resolution cryo-EM maps. The dataset comprises 972 nonredundant protein-chain samples from 495 cryo-EM protein structures resolved at 4.5-8.0 A, with voxel-level annotations for helices, sheets, and non-periodic secondary-structure (NPSS) regions. The dataset is stratified into three resolution ranges4.5-5.5, 5.5-6.5, and 6.5-8.0 Ato enable systematic analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance. Using this benchmark, we evaluate five representative convolutional and transformer-based volumetric segmentation architecturesU-Net, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, and Swin-UNETRunder standardized preprocessing, training, and evaluation protocols. Residual U-Net achieves the highest macro-averaged foreground (Macro-FG) F1 score in all three resolution bins, while helices are segmented more accurately than sheets and NPSS regions. All five architectures achieve their highest Macro-FG F1 scores in the highest-resolution bin, whereas performance varies between the two lower-resolution bins across architectures and secondary-structure classes. Overall, this benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance, supports reproducible method development, and facilitates controlled comparison of future cryo-EM secondary-structure segmentation approaches.

title: Ultrasound-assisted free radical grafting of sesamol onto whey protein isolate: Structural modifications, functional enhancements, and antioxidant properties.
authors: Feng, Xiandan; Lv, Mengting; Tian, Mu; Li, Sining; Tang, Shanhu
abstract: This study fabricated conjugates of whey protein isolate (WPI) and sesamol using an ultrasound-assisted free radical method. This approach significantly reduced the reaction time from 24 h to 90 min relative to the conventional free radical method, while achieving a comparable sesamol binding equivalent (4.65 mg/g). Structural analyses (amino acid side-chains, FTIR, XRD, surface hydrophobicity) revealed chemical modifications, as supported by reduced free thiol/amino groups and altered protein conformation under ultrasound. Molecular docking suggested potential hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions between sesamol and WPI. Particle size and zeta-potential measurements revealed formation of larger, stable aggregates. Furthermore, WPI-sesamol conjugates exhibited superior functional properties, including protein solubility and emulsifying capacity, as well as enhanced antioxidant activity (DPPH* and ABTS(+)* scavenging), with ultrasound-assisted treatment yielding the most pronounced improvements. The ultrasound-assisted method establishes an efficient strategy for producing WPI-sesamol conjugates with superior functionality and antioxidant capacity, highlighting their potential as novel food ingredients.

title: dictyBase 2026: a reimplementation of the Dictyostelium model organism database on minimal infrastructure.
authors: Mendieta, Maddox J; Dodson, Robert J; Basu, Siddhartha; Chisholm, Rex L; Scaglione, K Matthew
abstract: Dictyostelium discoideum is a model organism used to investigate a wide array of biological processes including chemotaxis, cell motility, phagocytosis, multicellular development, and autophagy. Many of its genes have human orthologs implicated in disease, making it a useful model organism for studying conditions ranging from cancer to neurodegeneration. dictyBase has served this community for two decades as a home for genomic data, protocols, a stock center, and community news. Here we describe a complete reimplementation of dictyBase as a self-contained service that uses static data files rather than a database server. Each gene record gathers curated function, human-disease context, developmental expression, and protein structure in a single webpage. The site also provides tools for sequence search, genome browsing, enrichment analysis, and experimental design. The complete Dicty Stock Center catalog of 7055 strains and 1265 plasmids is included, and both can be ordered from the site. New literature is curated by an author-in-the-loop pipeline. A language model drafts the annotations, the authors of the paper correct them, and a curator approves them. Analyses can be run on curator-approved annotations alone or extended to include those still awaiting review. dictyBase is freely available at https://dicty.org.

title: Artificial Intelligence-powered Advances in Phytomedicine: A Systematic Review on Plant-based Drug Discovery Software.
authors: Vig, Himangi; Wal, Ankita; Khanam, Zia; Nigam, Aditi; Pandey, Virat Kumar
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Herbal medicines contain complex phytochemicals that offer therapeutic potential, but their long-term adverse effects remain challenging to determine. Traditional herbal medicine preparation methods are often labor-intensive, non-standardized, and face difficulties in identifying active ingredients. By improving medication development, optimization, and discovery procedures, Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides innovative ways to get beyond these restrictions. This systematic review aims to evaluate the role of AI-based software such as LEAFSNAP, Deep- Chem, PlantNet, Autodock, MestReNova, XCMS, ADMETlab, SynergyFinder, KEGG, TCMID, and Reactome in enhancing phytomedicine research by streamlining plant identification, bioactive compound discovery, molecular modeling, and pharmacokinetic profiling, thereby advancing drug discovery and development processes. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA guidelines) to explore the integration of AI-based tools in phytomedicine research and drug discovery. Literature searches were performed in Scopus, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases, focusing on studies published between January 2015 and January 2025. Only English-language articles focusing on AI-based software for drug discovery from plant-derived compounds were reviewed. Studies discussing synthetic drug development were excluded; this, along with non-English language, acted as a literature review limitation. Two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the retrieved articles. Any discrepancies in the screening, study selection, and data extraction processes were resolved through discussion and consensus. RESULTS: Through the effective identification of bioactive chemicals and the simplification of intricate studies, the combination of artificial intelligence and computer tools has completely transformed the process of discovering and developing herbal drugs. DISCUSSION: Artificial intelligence tools like ADMETlab for pharmacokinetics and toxicity assessments, DeepChem for molecular activity modelling, and AlphaFold for protein structure prediction have greatly improved the search for new herbal drugs. While AutoDock improves molecular docking simulations by automating ligand-receptor binding predictions for bioactive chemicals, LeafSnap and PlantNet make plant identification simpler. Drug development workflows are improved by databases such as KEGG and TCMID, which combine pathway analysis with conventional medical knowledge. CONCLUSION: Research on phytomedicine may reach its full potential if AI techniques are improved and traditional knowledge and contemporary technology are better integrated.

title: Supramolecular assembly and membrane anchoring alter variant-induced SARS-CoV-2 Spike conformational dynamics.
authors: Gramm, Amanda J; Braet, Sean M; Srinivasu, Bindu Y; Venkatakrishnan, Varun; Bass, Elijah J; Kearns, Fiona L; Amaro, Rommie E; Stahelin, Robert V; Wales, Thomas E; Anand, Ganesh S
abstract: Viral surface glycoproteins function within crowded, membrane-anchored supramolecular assemblies, yet their dynamics are often inferred from soluble, engineered ectodomains. For SARS-CoV-2 Spike (S), this distinction is especially important because variant mutations evolved in the context of intact virions, not engineered trimers. Here, we combined cyclic ion mobility mass spectrometry (CIM-MS) for hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDXMS) with computational weighted ensemble molecular dynamic (WE-MD) simulations to compare the conformational effects of SARS-CoV-2 mutations in two S protein constructs: soluble recombinant 2P S and full-length S displayed in virus-like particles (VLPs). Our results reveal that membrane anchoring and virion-like assembly substantially dampen global dynamic changes produced by variant mutations. In VLP S, D614G induced decreased dynamics across interprotomer contacts, whereas Omicron BA.1 mutations systematically reversed this decrease in dynamics in the S1 domain while preserving decreased dynamics near the fusion machinery. These effects are more spatially constrained than those observed in recombinant 2P S. Comparison of the 2 constructs further reveals that 2P substitutions alter native interprotomer communication. Recombinant S shows a predominantly fast-exchanging population in the receptor binding domain (RBD) hinge region, consistent with disruption of hydrogen-bonding and salt bridge networks that couple RBD motion to the trimer core. Thus, recombinant S captures important structural features of S without recapitulating the native conformational ensemble presented on virions. Together, these results show that the supramolecular context of S reshapes the conformational dynamics of variant evolution with direct implications for epitope presentation, antibody recognition, and interpretation of recombinant S structural studies.

title: Macrocycle-Integrated MOF Nanoarchitectures: Cooperative Active Sites from Pillararenes, Calixarenes, and Crown Ethers.
authors: Mohan, Brij; Sharma, Harish Kumar; Najafov, Bakhtiyar; Garazade, Ismayil M; Seyidova, Khayala; Gupta, Rakesh Kumar; Virender, Virender; da Silva, M Fatima C Guedes; Pombeiro, Armando J L; Kim, Sang Sub
abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) offer crystalline porosity, modular structures, and tunable chemical environments, but they often lack the molecular recognition needed for highly selective adsorption, transport, and catalysis. Integrating macrocycles such as pillararenes, calixarenes, and crown ethers provides a route to macrocycle@MOF nanoarchitectures in which supramolecular cavities cooperate with framework pores, metal nodes, and linker functionalities. Calixarene-based MOFs create adaptive pockets for iodine capture, NO(2) sensing, and molecular separation; pillararene systems provide rigid, electron-rich channels for sieving, controlled release, and supramolecular docking; and crown-ether-functionalized MOFs enable selective ion transport, lithium sieving, and Sr(2+)/Cs(+) remediation. Their function arises from coupled host-guest recognition, pore confinement, electrostatic complementarity, and active-site organization. Key challenges include pore blocking, synthetic complexity, structural disorder, incomplete active-site validation, and device integration. This review highlights design principles for converting macrocycle-integrated MOFs from proof-of-concept materials into practical recognition platforms for advanced catalysis, separations, sensing, remediation, energy technologies, and biomedical applications.

title: Evaluating generative models for structure-based drug discovery from de novo design to lead optimization.
authors: Cao, Duanhua; Fan, Zhehuan; Yu, Jie; Chen, Mingan; Jiang, Xinyu; Sheng, Xia; Wang, Xingyou; Zeng, Chuanlong; Luo, Xiaomin; Teng, Dan; Zheng, Mingyue
abstract: Advances in protein structure prediction have created opportunities for structure-based drug design, yet translating structural knowledge into actionable small-molecule ligands remains difficult. Existing benchmarks often use simplified datasets and computational surrogates that poorly capture the heterogeneity and constraints of real-world drug discovery. We introduce MolGenBench, a comprehensive benchmark for de novo molecular generation and hit-to-lead optimization built on a large, structurally diverse dataset. Evaluation of 17 leading methods reveals persistent limitations, including weak virtual-screening performance, limited coverage of target-specific bioactive space, frequent high-risk structural motifs, poor target awareness, and reduced generalization to unseen proteins. Although some models improve three-dimensional conformation generation, they still struggle to produce active molecules reliably. MolGenBench provides standardized data, metrics, and analyses that connect structural prediction with practical molecular design and guide the development of more effective structure-based generative models.

title: SprintX: mitigating data scarcity in antibody design via synthetic structural prior knowledge dataset.
authors: Heo, Ryong; Lee, Dahyeon; Jung, Jaeho; Kim, Byung Ju; Park, Chihyun
abstract: Structure-based artificial intelligence (AI)-driven antibody design is increasingly important for therapeutic development, yet progress has been hindered by the scarcity of high-quality antibody-antigen complex structures for model training. To alleviate this bottleneck, we introduce SprintX (Structural Prior for Antibody-Antigen CompleXes), a large-scale AlphaFold3-derived synthetic dataset designed to provide structural prior knowledge for antibody-antigen modeling. Unlike conventional docking-based synthesis pipelines, SprintX uses AlphaFold3 to generate antigen-conditioned candidate complex-structure predictions from sampled antibody sequences paired with selected antigens, without imposing predefined binding-site or pose constraints. Candidate structures were ranked to select one representative structure per antibody-antigen pair before terminal trimming and multistage quality control. To improve reliability and learning stability, we applied a multi-stage quality-control pipeline integrating global confidence metrics, stereochemical validation, and interface-level contact analysis. SprintX recapitulated key geometric characteristics and physicochemical regularities of experimentally resolved antibody-antigen complexes while filtering out structurally unstable or implausible synthetic outputs. Across downstream tasks including antibody generation, computational binding-affinity prediction, and binding-interface prediction, models pretrained with SprintX showed meaningful improvements in structural plausibility and competitive performance on computational binding-affinity and binding-interface prediction benchmarks. These results support SprintX not as a substitute for experimentally resolved complexes, but as a complementary source of structural prior knowledge for structure-aware antibody modeling. Finally, we release SprintX as an openly accessible resource to facilitate data-efficient learning for AI-driven antibody design.

title: Stochastic and quantum perspectives on teleost immunity: Linking immunogenetics, structure, and biophysics.
authors: Abo-Al-Ela, Haitham G
journal: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology
abstract: Teleost fishes possess highly diverse, lineage-specific pattern-recognition receptor (PRR) repertoires shaped by teleost-specific whole-genome duplication (3R-WGD), subsequent duplication, differential retention, functional divergence, and gene loss. Toll-like, RIG-I-like, and NOD-like receptor families show lineage-specific expansion and, in some cases, adaptive sequence evolution, particularly in regions implicated in ligand recognition. Separately, hydrogen tunneling is supported in specific enzyme reactions, while radical-pair chemistry provides a bounded mechanistic precedent rather than evidence for teleost immune function. This review examines whether teleost PRR diversification creates concrete, testable opportunities for investigating analogous biophysical mechanisms, without assuming that receptor diversity or environmental sensitivity entails non-classical effects. A five-level evidence hierarchy is applied: direct teleost evidence, evidence from other systems, indirect teleost evidence, testable hypothesis, and unsupported or contradicted claim. No direct evidence was identified for a functionally consequential quantum-biological mechanism in teleost immune recognition or signaling. However, increasing genomic, structural, transcriptomic, single-cell, and functional-genomic resolution provides a tractable framework for testing such possibilities. Sequence and structural divergence among PRR paralogs can be evaluated using structure prediction, molecular dynamics, and, where chemically justified, quantum-chemical or QM/MM methods, with uncertainty assessed across stages and experimental validation through ligand binding, signaling, and environmental-response phenotypes. The NADPH-to-flavin hydride-transfer step in an immune effector oxidase is proposed as a chemically defined candidate, not an established teleost tunneling mechanism. Quantum mechanisms therefore remain hypotheses rather than established features of teleost immunity. A falsifiable research roadmap is proposed linking receptor evolution to structure-function relationships, signaling diversity, redox processes, and candidate quantum-sensitive molecular events.

title: Salt-Mediated Long-Range Electrostatic Signature of Native Binding Surface Pre-Organizes Bound-Like Conformations of p53 C-Terminal Intrinsically Disordered Region.
authors: Das, Kingshuk; Jana, Biman
journal: Chemphyschem : a European journal of chemical physics and physical chemistry
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs) often undergo a disorder-to-order transition via coupled folding and binding. The p53 C-terminal domain (CTD) IDR folds into a helical conformation upon binding S100B, yet the long-range influence of the ionic environment on this transition remains poorly understood. Using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with a novel confinement setup, we investigated the conformational landscape of a 12-residue fragment of p53 CTD at varying distances from the S100B binding cleft. Comparing behavior in pure water and physiological salt (150 mM NaCl), we find that at 10 A from the native binding surface, the peptide spontaneously forms stable, bound-like helical segments exclusively in the salt solution. This effect is distance-dependent, vanishing at 20 A, and specific to the native binding surface, notably occurring without direct protein-IDR contacts. Our results demonstrate that the negatively charged S100B surface organizes solvated ions into a structured, long-range electrostatic microenvironment that thermodynamically stabilizes bound-like helical conformations prior to direct contact. This reveals a synergistic effect between native surface topology and physiological salt that biases the IDR's conformational ensemble to facilitate binding, identifying the ions in the solution as active participants in molecular recognition.

title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85.
authors: Briggs, David C; Duffy, Ryan T; Ateaque, Sarah; Maslen, Sarah; Nagaraj, Hema; Barde, Yves-Alain; DiStefano, Peter S; Lindsay, Ronald M; Armstrong, Paul C; Peach, Chloe J; McDonald, Neil Q
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.

title: Pseudoknots: Based RRI Detection Using Machine Learning Models.
authors: Joel, W; Varadarajan, Swetha
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are fundamental to diverse cellular processes, including gene regulation, RNA splicing, editing, and translation. These interactions, whether intra- or inter-molecular, contribute to RNA functionality and cellular regulatory networks. A major structural component influencing RRIs is the presence of pseudoknots-non-nested base-pairing interactions that are critical to the function of ribozymes, viral RNAs, telomerase, and ribosomal RNA. Despite their biological importance, pseudoknots are frequently excluded from computational models due to the increased complexity they introduce to RNA secondary structure prediction and interaction detection. Traditional dynamic programming algorithms are limited to pseudoknot-free models, resulting in many RNA-RNA interaction prediction tools simplifying or ignoring pseudoknots altogether. This oversimplification can compromise the accuracy of predictions, particularly in scenarios where pseudoknotted structures are essential for biological function. Recent advancements in machine learning (ML) and deep learning offer new potential to model such complex RNA features. By leveraging large-scale sequence and structural data, ML models can implicitly learn interaction patterns associated with pseudoknotted regions, offering improved predictive power over thermodynamics-based methods alone. This chapter explores how pseudoknot-aware modeling can be integrated into ML-based RRI detection pipelines. We discuss the biological relevance of pseudoknots, computational challenges in modeling them, and the strategies for designing and extracting features that capture pseudoknot structures. We also survey current ML approaches, including classical and deep learning models, and examine how they incorporate structural information. Case studies are presented to demonstrate practical applications, followed by a review of benchmarking methods, datasets, and performance evaluation strategies. By combining biologically informed structure prediction with advanced ML techniques, this chapter outlines a framework for improving the fidelity of RRI detection in the presence of pseudoknots.

title: LSTM-Based Methods for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
authors: Ramachandran, Akhilesh; Varadarajan, Swetha
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are central to various biological processes, including post-transcriptional regulation, gene silencing, and viral replication. While traditional computational methods for RRI prediction rely on sequence complementarity and thermodynamic models, deep learning approaches, particularly those leveraging long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown great promise in modeling the complexity of RNA behavior. This chapter reviews recent advances in LSTM-based methods for RRI prediction, discusses the key datasets and evaluation metrics, and outlines future directions in this emerging field.

title: Using the Function Prediction Server and Queryome for Functional Protein Design.
authors: Punuru, Pranav; Giri, Swagarika; Kihara, Daisuke
abstract: Accurate computational prediction of protein function is critical for guiding the functional design of proteins in the post-genomic era. The gap between the number of protein sequences deposited in databases and those with experimentally validated functional annotations continues to widen, making automated function prediction tools indispensable for researchers. In this chapter, we describe a suite of complementary computational tools for protein function prediction and literature-based functional analysis. We cover four sequence-based Gene Ontology (GO) term prediction methods available through the Protein Function Prediction web server: PFP, ESG (Extended Similarity Group), Phylo-PFP, and Domain-PFP. Each method leverages distinct algorithmic strategies, from mining distantly related sequences with PSI-BLAST to recursive multilevel sequence searches, phylogenetic distance-based reranking, and function-aware domain embeddings. We also describe Queryome, a multi-agent deep research system that performs evidence-grounded synthesis across 28.3 million PubMed abstracts, which can be used to contextualize and validate function predictions with primary literature evidence. We provide step-by-step protocols for using these tools, interpreting results, and integrating predictions into a workflow for the functional design of proteins. The Protein function prediction server is available at www.kiharalab.org/pfp and Queryome is available as a desktop application at www.queryome.app.

title: An Effective Pipeline to Develop Modification-Specific Intracellular Antibodies Using AI Tools.
authors: Maejima, Daiki; Galindo, Gabriel; Stasevich, Timothy J; Kimura, Hiroshi
abstract: Posttranslational protein modifications (PTMs) are often associated with protein functions. To detect PTMs in living cells, genetically encoded antibody-based probes, termed modification-specific intracellular antibodies (mintbodies), have been developed. A mintbody consists of a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of a modification-specific antibody and a fluorescent protein. By expressing mintbodies in cells or organisms, the localization and changes in the specifically modified form of a protein can be tracked in real time. In particular, mintbodies against histone and RNA polymerase II PTMs have been developed and are available. However, most mouse monoclonal antibodies fail to remain functional when expressed in the reduced environment inside eukaryotic cells due to unstable folding. This results in an inability to bind antigen, instability, aggregation, and/or degradation. Whereas there have been no general methods to develop functional intracellular antibodies, we have recently developed a convenient pipeline to efficiently convert unstable scFvs into stable and functional probes using AI-assisted tools. We here describe a practical, end-to-end protocol for converting existing antibody sequences into functional intracellular antibodies using an AI-assisted design pipeline combined with live-cell screening. The method integrates antibody sequence annotation, structure prediction, deep-learning-based framework optimization, and experimental validation in mammalian cells.

title: PNPShift: an NMR chemical shift predictor for purine-nucleotide-bound and unliganded proteins.
authors: Zeng, Mingfei; Liu, Dan; Shui, Leilei; Wang, Hao; Long, Dong
abstract: Accurate prediction of protein chemical shifts is important for NMR-based structural and ensemble modeling. However, most existing predictors are designed for unliganded proteins and cannot quantitatively calculate the chemical shifts of purine nucleotide-bound proteins, which are encoded by approximately 10% of the human genome and play critical roles in signal transduction, energy metabolism, and other cellular processes. Here, we introduce PNPShift, an artificial neural network-based program designed to improve chemical shift prediction accuracy for purine nucleotide-bound proteins. By incorporating the PNPShift-X(PN) correction, PNPShift reduces (1)H(N) prediction errors in nucleotide-binding regions by up to ~ 30% across 28 tested purine nucleotide-bound proteins. PNPShift also improves (1)H(N) predictions for unliganded proteins, achieving a ~ 6% reduction in RMSE across an independent test set of 60 proteins. The utility of PNPShift in structural and dynamics modeling is demonstrated by its superior performance in maximum-entropy (MEM)-based ensemble refinement and its greater ability to discriminate native states from decoy conformations compared with other leading programs. PNPShift not only extends accurate chemical-shift prediction to purine nucleotide-bound proteins critical for diverse cellular functions, but also illustrates a general framework for developing predictors for other liganded protein systems.

title: A Metadynamics-Based Protocol for Sampling and Scoring Peptide Nanofibril Conformations.
authors: Yang, Chao-Yu; Miller, Aline F; Saiani, Alberto; Bryce, Richard A
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: The morphology of a cross-beta nanofibril, ranging from ribbon to rod conformations, is commonly determined by the amino acid sequence of its constituent peptides in addition to environmental factors such as pH and salt concentration. The use of all-atom molecular dynamics simulation of a given peptide nanofibril to explore its energetically favorable fibril conformations is a desirable but challenging goal, due to potential trapping in local energy minima. In this work, we explore a metadynamics-based approach to investigate morphologically distinct peptide nanofibrils, introducing collective variables based on supramolecular twist as a sampling coordinate. We artificially construct a search space consistent with integral fibril structures and perform metadynamics simulations to overcome energy barriers and traverse the rugged conformational landscape of the large peptide assemblies in water. Based on this, we compute a measure which we term the resistance score to identify the propensity of distinct fibril morphologies across the conformational space. This computational protocol is then used to investigate the impact of fibril length and peptide sequence on the supramolecular twist of peptide nanofibrils in aqueous solution, comparing these results with the fibril morphologies observed in electron microscopy. The proposed workflow demonstrates an ability to identify a preferred morphology for beta-sheet assemblies, which could aid in the design of new peptide self-assembled architectures.

title: Multiscale Modeling of Lytic Polysaccharide Monooxygenases in Oxidized and Reduced Redox States.
authors: Szleper-Shendy, Katarzyna; Escorcia, Andres M; Kumar, Ravi; Gora, Artur; Stein, Matthias
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) are copper-dependent oxidative enzymes whose catalytic activity depends on redox cycling of a single copper ion in the active site, coordinated by the conserved histidine brace motif. Although the static coordination geometry of the active site has been characterized crystallographically, the dynamic response of the histidine brace to Cu(I)/Cu(II) cycling and the role of second-sphere residues in modulating this response remain poorly understood at the atomistic level. Here, we address this gap using a multiscale computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, QM/MM optimization, and EPR parameter calculations, applied to two representative LPMOs: NcAA9C (AA9, axial tyrosine) and BaAA10A (AA10, axial phenylalanine). The structural response to the change in oxidation state is seen almost entirely in the exogenous ligands rather than in the histidine brace itself, with the oxidized form showing markedly higher and longer-lived water coordination. In BaAA10A, the equatorial water is anchored by a second-sphere glutamate with no counterpart in NcAA9C. QM/MM electrostatic perturbation analysis identifies Asp76 (NcAA9C) and Glu68 (BaAA10A) as the dominant stabilizing residues of the catalytic core, acting through water-mediated hydrogen-bond bridges that are more pronounced in the Cu(II) state. Computed EPR parameters respond to the displacement of the copper site from a planar geometry, and the equatorial water position was shown to have the dominant effect, differentiating the two LPMOs.

title: A Microscopic View of Protein Soft and Reactive Landing on Flexible Polyethylene Glycol Surfaces.
authors: Bertolini, Samuel; Delcorte, Arnaud
abstract: The interaction of proteins with polymer surfaces is central to understanding biomaterial compatibility and developing advanced deposition techniques. In this work, we investigate the collision dynamics of lysozyme and neurotensin with polyethylene glycol (PEG) surfaces in the vacuum using the reactive force field (ReaxFF). These simulations mimic the soft and reactive landing processes encountered in electrospray ionization (ESI)-, matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)- and cluster ion beam-based preparative mass spectrometry approaches. Various PEG structures, including vertically aligned chains and amorphous configurations, with or without surface chain terminations, were considered. Collision velocities ranging from 1 to 6 km/s were employed to explore structural preservation, energy transfer, and chemical bond formation between the biomolecules and the PEG. For lysozyme ( approximately 14 kDa), where 1 km/s corresponds to approximately 74 eV, our results show that PEG acts as a soft, cushion-like substrate, effectively dissipating impact energy and preserving protein structure under most conditions. Notably, covalent bond formation was observed only at high velocity (>/=5 km/s) in the amorphous PEG structure lacking surface chain terminations. The findings indicate that PEG offers a promising medium for preserving protein integrity during deposition, maintaining the capacity to build protein multilayers, and potentially facilitating controlled protein desorption in solvents when desired. Even though defining an exact energy threshold would require a more detailed investigation, our simulations also constitute a proof-of-principle that the molecular fragments also transferred in iBEAM may act as mediators to induce protein grafting at relatively low velocity (3 km/s).

title: Identification of a novel equine rotavirus B from Missouri in 2025, which is distantly related to group B rotaviruses.
authors: Soni, Shalini; Hause, Ben; Uprety, Tirth; Yu, Jieshi; Shuisong, Ni; Eertink, Lianne G; Fang, Zheng; Giri, Kripa; Erdal, Erol; Morgan, Jocelynn; Lawson, Steven; Nelson, Eric; Graves, Amy J; Morrow, Jennifer K; Adam, Emma N; Sheng, Zizhang; Kennedy, Michael A; Wang, Dan; Li, Feng
abstract: Despite the wide circulation of group B rotaviruses in animals and humans, rotavirus B was not found in horses until 2021 in Kentucky, USA. Little is known about the genetic diversity and evolution of rotavirus B in this new host. Here, we described a divergent equine rotavirus B (ERVB) from a foal with idiopathic diarrhea in Missouri (designated MO-ERVB-25). Full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that MO-ERVB-25 is distantly related to all previously known group B rotaviruses, including ERVB strains identified in 2021 in Kentucky (KY-ERVB-21). The mean nucleotide substitution rate of the VP4 segment was estimated as 1.44 x 10(-3) substitutions/site/year, which is a magnitude higher than the VP7 segment. We further demonstrated that MO-ERVB-25, like human RVB, binds chemically neutral LacNAc-containing complex N-linked glycans, while KY-ERVB-21 recognizes negatively charged polysialic acid (polySia) with alpha-2,8-linkage, which is a functional receptor for unrelated enteric human adenovirus 52. Using the AlphaFold-enabled structure prediction, we showed that both MO-ERVB-25 and human RVB VP8* lack a novel C-terminal alpha2 helix that is only observed in the KY-ERVB-21 VP8*, which may help explain the difference in glycan binding specificities. Finally, screening of foal samples by the reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay identified 4.2% of idiopathic foal diarrhea samples (6 out of 140) positive for MO-ERVB-25. These results suggest that MO-ERVB-25 represents a new rotavirus B subgroup that circulates in foals. Its circulation, together with KY-ERVB-25 subgroup, raises the possibility of reassortment and antigenic shift as mechanisms of rotavirus B evolution in equines. IMPORTANCE: Equine RVB (ERVB) has emerged as a significant cause of foal diarrhea since 2021. Our study describes a highly divergent RVB strain identified in a foal with severe diarrhea in 2025. This ERVB variant exhibited low amino acid identity compared with previously reported ERVB strains. The novel ERVB strain escaped routine diagnostic detection. Sequence analysis demonstrated that this new strain grouped with bovine, porcine, caprine, and equine RVB but formed a distinct, independent branch. In addition, glycan array studies revealed the substantial difference in glycan recognition between new and previously described ERVB strains, which is likely determined by the presence or absence of a novel C-terminal alpha2 helix in the VP8* receptor-binding domain. These results suggest that this novel ERVB variant may co-circulate with existing ERVB strains in horses, which may facilitate rapid viral evolution through antigenic diversity, a property previously reported in rotaviruses from other hosts.

title: Metal-ion coordination drives active-site remodeling for backsplicing in circularly permuted group II introns.
authors: Zhang, Jie; Yao, Yuqi; Ma, Jinbiao
abstract: Circularly permuted (CP) group II introns are self-splicing ribozymes that undergo a sequential branching and backsplicing reaction to yield branched introns and circular exons (circRNAs). While the initial branching step is structurally characterized, the mechanistic principles that govern the subsequent large-scale active-site remodeling and stringent metal-ion specificity required for backsplicing remain poorly understood. Here, we present a series of high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the CP group II intron from Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus PAL5 (Gdi-1), capturing the ribozyme at discrete stages along the branching -to- backsplicing pathway under distinct ionic conditions. Comparative analyses under K+/Mg2+, K+/Ca2+, and Cs+/Mg2+ conditions demonstrate that productive backsplicing relies on ion-specific coordination networks that govern 3' splice site (3'SS) docking and catalytic center formation, revealing the precise metal-ion-coordinated conformational rearrangements and dynamic splice-site exchange mechanisms. Crucially, we identify a previously unrecognized, highly selective monovalent cation-binding site, K3, that structurally couples the gamma-gamma' interaction to reassembly of the heteronuclear four-metal core, thereby promoting productive second-step active-site formation. Together, these findings establish a structural basis for metal-ion-dependent active-site remodeling during group II intron catalysis and provide mechanistic insights into metal-ion selectivity in circRNA biogenesis.

title: Prediction of Residue-Level Base Preference for DNA-Binding Proteins Using a Multimodal Learning Framework.
authors: Li, Siyuan; He, Wenyan; Zhang, Mengru; Zhang, Xin; Fang, Wei-Qun; Xu, Min-Juan; Shi, Yi; Cai, Yujia; Zhang, Yong; Da, Lin-Tai
abstract: Specific recognition between proteins and DNA governs essential cellular functions, yet the binding specificity of most DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) remains experimentally uncharacterized and high-throughput experimental methods still lag far behind the ever-growing protein data set. Here, we present 3M-BSIP (3-modal base-specific interaction predictor), a multimodal deep learning framework capable of predicting the DNA-binding interface and residue-level base preference for DBPs. 3M-BSIP constructs a holistic protein representation by integrating three distinct modalities: a protein language model capturing evolutionary conservation; a graph neural network encoding 3D structural features; and a hierarchical encoder characterizing physicochemical properties of protein surface pointclouds. Comprehensive benchmarking demonstrates that 3M-BSIP achieves SOTA performance on both interface-residue identification and base-preference predictions. Crucially, the model maintains robust performance on computationally constructed protein structures and is also tolerant toward those undergoing profound structural rearrangements upon DNA binding. Two real-world applications of 3M-BSIP demonstrate that our model not only can accurately predict the specific binding motif of structurally unknown transcription factors but also, more importantly, can guide rapid reprogramming of the base preference of DBPs based on a purely computational pipeline. Therefore, 3M-BSIP holds great potential in annotating the binding motifs of all DBPs in a high-throughput manner and designing new DBPs with desired base specificities.

title: Reshaping the scissors: From directed evolution to AI-driven design for enhanced Cas performance.
authors: Cheng, Xinrui; Ruan, Weimin; Jin, Zheng; Suo, Langda; Ma, Yuehui; Jiang, Lin; Zheng, Wenxin; Li, Ning; Hu, Wenping
abstract: CRISPR/Cas gene editing holds great promise for applications in agricultural breeding and gene therapy; however, native Cas proteins face bottlenecks such as off-target effects, PAM limitations, and delivery challenges. This review explores a three-tiered, progressive, and synergistic analytical framework comprising directed evolution, rational structural design, and integrated protein engineering. Following the logic of "random exploration-precision modification-system integration," it systematically clarifies the principles, advantages, disadvantages, and complementary interactions among these three optimization techniques. By comprehensively mapping the entire technical pathway for Cas protein improvement, this study fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field and provides a theoretical framework for tiered, synergistic modification to support the development of high-performance editors. The paper further analyzes a novel research and development paradigm in which AI and protein language models profoundly empower Cas modification. It summarizes intelligent toolchains such as structure prediction, virtual mutation, and de novo design of artificial Cas proteins, and highlights the unique advantages of AI in overcoming the performance trade-offs inherent in traditional protein engineering. At the same time, it identifies existing challenges, such as data scarcity and insufficient model interpretability, and looks ahead to how multimodal gene-editing large language models and automated closed-loop experimental systems will drive the iterative development of miniaturized, broad-spectrum, and highly precise editing tools, thereby facilitating the clinical and industrial implementation of gene-editing technologies.

title: A dual-function XCL1-CD40L mRNA adjuvant potentiates cancer vaccines by coordinating DC recruitment and maturation.
authors: Wu, Chunjie; Shao, Wanxuan; Liu, Yadi; Pan, Shuyuan; Wang, Wei; Deng, Li; Zhang, Suyue; Cui, Zhimin; Wang, Yujiao; He, Peng; Yang, Yong; Zhao, Yiheng
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite the significant promise of mRNA tumor vaccines in treating solid tumors, their clinical response rate is constrained by the low effectiveness of antigen presentation resulting from the immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1) are pivotal in antigen cross-presentation; yet, they frequently exhibit insufficient immune-activating communication within solid malignancies. METHODS: This investigation comprehensively examined the functional attributes of cDC1 by TCGA cohorts and single-cell transcriptomic data. Guided by these bioinformatic insights, we engineered and synthesized a dual-functional mRNA adjuvant encoding the mXCL1-mCD40L fusion protein. We assessed the biological functions and anti-tumor efficacy of this adjuvant in combination with Glypican-3 (GPC3) and HPV-associated mRNA vaccines via protein expression, structure prediction, in vivo antigen uptake and presentation assays, antigen-presenting cell activation assays, antigen-specific T cell activation tests, and therapeutic studies in tumor-bearing mouse models. RESULTS: A high cDC1 signature score was associated with improved overall survival across LIHC and SKCM TCGA cohorts. Compared to normal sample, cDC1s in HCC and melanoma retained their antigen-presentation machinery but received reduced activating ligand inputs (XCL1-XCR1 signaling in HCC and CD40-CD40L signaling in melanoma). AlphaFold 3 showed that the mXCL1-mCD40L fusion protein can maintain structural integrity without spatial steric hindrance. The fusion protein was confirmed to be secreted and to retain both XCL1-dependent chemotactic activity and CD40-dependent dendritic-cell activation. mXCL1-mCD40L mRNA-LNP activated macrophages and dendritic cells in vitro, upregulating immune-related gene expression as confirmed by qPCR. In vivo, the dual-functional adjuvant significantly enhanced the anti-tumor effect of the GPC3 vaccine, outperformed co-delivery of separate mXCL1 and mCD40L mRNA-LNP, and induced stronger specific IFN-gamma producing T cells. Meanwhile, this adjuvant also boosted the anti-tumor efficacy of HPV-associated mRNA vaccines. Mechanistically, this adjuvant increased tumor-antigen acquisition and cross-presentation by CD103(+) DCs and promoted DC maturation in draining lymph nodes, accompanied by an increased proportion of peripheral CD8(+) T cells.
