CONCLUSION: By enhancing the recruitment and maturation of cDC1s, the dual-function mXCL1-mCD40L mRNA adjuvant boosts the efficacy of GPC3 and HPV-associated mRNA vaccines, supporting its potential as an antigen-flexible adjuvant platform against solid tumors.

title: Explorations of the Hydrogenation of D(2) by Nitrogenase.
authors: Dance, Ian
journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology
abstract: A non-physiological substrate of the enzyme nitrogenase, D(2), is doubly hydrogenated by the enzyme to produce 2HD. This 'HD reaction' is in competition with the native function of the enzyme, hydrogenating N(2) to NH(3). At the active site of the enzyme, a gallery of H atom donors is identified, and the proposed complete cycle mechanism for the N(2) reaction uses these donors eight times to generate the 2NH(3) + H(2) products. Here, the functionality of these H atom donors in hydrogenating D(2) to 2HD is investigated, applying density functional simulations to a 480+ atom model of the active site including all important surrounds. Many possible reaction trajectories were explored, and a revised mechanism for the HD reaction is presented. The mechanisms for hydrogenation of D(2) and of N(2) have common components, accounting for their experimentally known competition. Consideration of ten items of relevant experimental data about the HD reaction shows how the proposed mechanism complies with and interprets these data, although two experimental observations are still to be checked.

title: A conserved insect transcobalamin-like gene is associated with vitamin B12-related functions in the silkworm Bombyx mori.
authors: Xiang, Jia-Hao; Wu, Yan; Xie, Qin-Hui; Chen, Bao-Zhen; Yi, Mei-Yan; Li, Fang-Yi; Tong, Xiao-Ling; Feng, Qi-Li; Wang, Man; Xiang, Hui
abstract: Vitamin B12 (VB12, cobalamin) is delivered by transcobalamin-dependent pathways in mammals, but comparable host-encoded factors and functions in insects remain unclear. Here we identify a single transcobalamin-like gene in the silkworm Bombyx mori ( Bmtcn) and detect homologs across diverse insect orders. Structure prediction and docking suggest that insect transcobalamin (TCN)-like proteins retain a conserved fold and a pocket compatible with cobalamin binding, although direct biochemical validation remains needed. Bmtcn expression is enriched in the head and is detectable across neuronal and glial populations, implicating the nervous system as a potential site of cobalamin handling and/or demand. Bmtcn loss-of-function mutants accumulate homocysteine, display behavioral abnormalities, and show brain-associated phenotypes. Head transcriptomics reveals coordinated changes consistent with perturbed folate-one-carbon metabolism and broad remodeling of core cellular programs alongside stress-associated responses in the mutants. Because insects lack canonical cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase, these findings suggest that cobalamin may act through alternative metabolic and/or signaling routes. Together, our results implicate a conserved insect transcobalamin-like component in vitamin B12-linked physiology and B. mori as a tractable system for mechanistic dissection.

title: Cooperative nature of residue interactions in biomolecular condensates.
authors: Chen, Le; Wu, Xiangyu; Hu, Guorong; Zeng, Xiangze; Li, Jingyuan
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Cooperativity of residue interactions is prevalent in proteins and plays an essential role in protein folding. However, whether cooperativity exists in intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their assembled biomolecular condensates remains elusive. Here, we reveal the presence of residue interaction cooperativity in various IDP condensates using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. In all these condensates, cooperative residue interactions manifest as packing between finite residue motifs (3 to 5 residues) with lifetimes three orders of magnitude longer than residue contacts. Notably, these higher-order interactions (HOIs) exhibit a significant nonadditive free energy, which originates from a local low-dielectric environment. The underlying sequence patterns like "Y-X-Q", "D-X-R", and "S-Y-X" are identified. Furthermore, HOIs dominate the cohesive energy of IDPs and condensates can be treated as HOI-crosslinked networks. This model can successfully reproduce experimental results of condensate physical properties, including saturation concentration, viscoelasticity, and interfacial tension.

title: Spatially Partitioned Engineering of an Alginate Lyase Overcomes the Stability-Activity Trade-Off via Distal Cap Loop Rigidification and Network Remodeling.
authors: Zhao, Mengxuan; Zhao, Mengqi; Zhang, Peiyi; Fan, Liqiang; Li, Xu; Deng, Chen; Zhao, Liming
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: The stability-activity trade-off limits engineering of alginate lyases for alginate oligosaccharide production. Here, a spatially partitioned semirational strategy coupled with the greedy accumulated strategy for protein engineering (GRAPE) was applied to an alginate lyase from Vibrio sp. The optimized variant M13 achieved a 4.6-fold increase in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) and an 11.4-fold extension of half-life at 50  degrees C. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that distal Cap Loop rigidification suppresses thermal unfolding while Gate Loop flexibility is retained for catalysis. A67K reversion increased Cap Loop flexibility and shifted the optimal temperature from 40 to 30  degrees C, supporting its thermostability contribution. Residue interaction network analysis identified a Val272-Tyr260-Arg73 communication pathway associated with active site preorganization into a near-attack conformation. V272A reversion reduced kcat/Km by 45.7%, supporting its catalytic contribution. These findings show that spatial partitioning can concurrently improve thermostability and catalytic efficiency, providing a design principle for polysaccharide lyase engineering.

title: Structure-Guided Engineering of Cu/Zn Superoxide Dismutase for Enhanced Catalytic Efficiency and Thermostability.
authors: Al-Adeeb, Abdulqader; Muhammad Aqeel, Sahibzada; Al-Jaberi, Hend Sadeq; Gu, Qiuya; Al-Ansi, Waleed; Al-Maqtari, Qais Ali; Liu, Wen-Long; Yu, Xiaobin
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn-SOD) is a key antioxidant enzyme that catalyzes superoxide radical dismutation. Here, an integrated computational-assisted, structure-guided engineering strategy was applied to improve Cu/Zn-SOD catalytic performance. Gln22 and Glu134 were identified as promising engineering sites, and saturation mutagenesis yielded Q22I and E134 M as the most beneficial single substitutions, with specific activities 1.55- and 2.39-fold higher than wild type (WT), respectively. Combining both substitutions generated M2 (Q22I/E134M), which showed the highest specific activity of 7121.0 U mg-1, corresponding to a 3.43-fold increase over WT. The optimal temperature of Q22I and M2 increased from 40 to 50  degrees C, and M2 also exhibited enhanced thermostability. Kinetic analysis showed that M2 had a 41.18% lower Km and a 2.95-fold higher Vmax than WT. Molecular docking suggested complementary effects of Q22I and E134 M on structural stability and active-site optimization, supporting improved catalytic performance. These findings provide a basis for engineering efficient, thermostable SODs.

title: Application of computational methods in the drug discovery and development of Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Zhang, Qianqian; Gong, Xiaoqing; Liu, Huanxiang; Yao, Xiaojun
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to cognitive decline. As the most common dementia, AD affects over 50 million individuals worldwide, with 10 million new cases each year. Despite many significant progresses in AD research fields, there is still no effective treatment. Advances in molecular modelling and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm have facilitated the application of computational methods in AD drug development, offering advantages in terms of efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and resource conservation. These strategies, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, and de novo drug design, have been widely employed in the past decades. Additionally, AI pharmaceutical companies have revolutionized the traditional drug development pipeline such as AD biomarker discovery, accurate diagnosis and precision medicine, etc. This review offers a thorough summary of recent progresses in computational-based methodologies in the study of AD drug development, including the elucidation the pathological mechanism at the molecular level, target identification, target 3D structure prediction, lead compound discovery, de novo molecular generation, multi-target directed ligands, drug repurposing, biomarker discovery, etc., showing promising applications of molecular modelling and AI in the development of AD therapy.

title: Future of cardiac diffusion magnetic resonance imaging: a bibliometric analysis.
authors: Wu, Xinyi; Yang, Yuelong; Xu, Yongzhou; Wu, Zhigang; Liu, Hui; Chen, Rui
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiac diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (cDMRI) has become a valuable noninvasive tool for assessing cardiac microstructure. OBJECTIVE: To perform a systematic and comprehensive bibliometric analysis of cDMRI to explore current status, research hotspots and potential future directions. MATERIAL AND METHODS: A systematic search of Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and PubMed was conducted to identify articles on cDMRI published between 2005 and 2024. All retrieved records were independently screened by two reviewers to exclude the articles unrelated to the topic about cDMRI. Co-citation, collaboration networks, burst keywords, and reference analyses were performed. RESULTS: There were 359 articles searched in WoSCC and 88 articles in PubMed. Finally, 367 articles met the search criteria in both databases. The cardiac "diffusion tensor imaging" (cDTI) emerged as the most prominent keyword, with the highest occurrence count (191.0) and strongest citation bursts (6.8). The study by Nielles-Vallespin et al. showed the strongest citation burst (26.17), accumulating 163 total citations and an average of 20.38 citations per year, highlighting its substantial influence on the development of cDMRI research. The top-cited articles with the strongest citation bursts concentrated on the clinical application of cDTI, its sequence design, and cardiac electrophysiology based on cDTI. The trend topic analysis further revealed "deep learning" as an emerging research focus in cDMRI since 2022. CONCLUSIONS: To our knowledge, this is the first dedicated bibliometric analysis focusing on cDMRI. By systematically analyzing the current status, research hotspots, and future trends of cDMRI, it provided valuable insights to guide future investigations in this field.

title: Structural basis of stepwise G protein activation by the viral chemokine receptor US28.
authors: Jude, Kevin M; Suomivuori, Carl-Mikael; Waghray, Deepa; Maeda, Shoji; Fujiyoshi, Yoshinori; Inoue, Asuka; Garcia, K Christopher; Tsutsumi, Naotaka
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) govern diverse cellular responses and are crucial drug targets. However, the sequence of structural events from G protein recognition to GDP release has remained elusive. Here, we leveraged the viral chemokine GPCR US28 to capture multiple activation states of the US28-G(q) complex. Using cryo-electron microscopy and an engineered chemokine superagonist, we determined three distinct complex structures, capturing a GDP-bound Encounter state, the nucleotide-free Canonical state, and a putative intermediate bridging the two states, the Transition-to-Canonical state. These structures, along with simulations and functional data, provide high-resolution snapshots of a plausible G protein activation trajectory and support a stepwise conformational model for G protein activation. This activation cascade closely parallels mechanisms proposed for human GPCRs, suggesting a conserved GPCR signaling mechanism.

title: Hierarchical Zeolites: Synthesis Strategies, Crystallization Mechanisms, and Machine Learning.
authors: Liu, Xingyuan; Qi, Xinyu; Li, Yang; Cong, Haifeng; Dai, Chengyi; Li, Xingang
abstract: The revelation of the crystallization mechanism of zeolites is the key to shifting their synthesis from trial-and-error methods to predictive approaches. This review introduces the traditional and recently emerging green synthesis methods of hierarchical zeolites and compares their crystallization mechanisms from the perspective of synthesis strategies. Then, by discussing the classical and nonclassical theories, it analyzes the crystallization mechanisms of different synthesis strategies for hierarchical zeolites and finds that the research on kinetic control methods not only conforms to the theme of green and environmentally friendly synthesis at present but also can further explore the mechanism of zeolite crystallization. Finally, this review also presents the research results of the emerging machine learning-assisted zeolite structure design, which will bring new possibilities for the future realization of hierarchical zeolite structure design and directed synthesis through predictive methods.

title: Contribution of disordered regions of the essential protein GEMIN5 to RNA binding.
authors: Francisco-Velilla, Rosario; Nahavandi Araghi, Azadeh; Ramajo, Jorge; Abellan, Salvador; Martinez-Salas, Encarnacion
abstract: GEMIN5 is emerging as a multifunctional RNA-binding protein (RBP) linked to human disease. This RBP comprises a WD40 repeat domain at the N terminus. The C-terminal region (G5C) includes a tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR)-like dimerization module, a non-canonical RNA-binding site (RBS), and an intrinsically disordered region (IDR). Understanding the molecular basis for RNA binding is critical to decipher how GEMIN5 pathological variants impact on their functions. Here we show that the RNA-binding domain consists of an extended binding surface comprising a serine-rich loop and an acidic cluster within the IDR. The RNA binding ability measured in vitro and in soluble cellular extracts indicated that individually, ser-rich motif and acidic cluster mutants diminished RNA binding intensity. However, in the absence of the RBS region, the TPR-extended protein is sufficient to facilitate RNA binding. AlphaFold modeling of the TPR-extended protein shows the assembly of an elongated dimer bound to RNA. The same RBS is observed in the G5C-RNA oligomer model. We propose that the elongated dimer forms an extended binding surface, fine-tuning the RNA binding ability of the G5C architecture.

title: pH-dependent structural dynamics and catalytic function of human thymidine kinase 1.
authors: Imtiyaz, Khadija; Haider, Nabeel; Saifi, Sana; Khan, Mohd Kaif; Noor, Saba; Alajmi, Mohamed F; Khan, Faez Iqbal; Khan, Nida Jamil; Hassan, Md Imtaiyaz
abstract: Human thymidine kinase 1 (hTK1) is a key enzyme in the thymidine salvage pathway that regulates DNA synthesis and repair and serves as an important biomarker of cellular proliferation and cancer. However, the influence of pH on its structural stability and catalytic function remains poorly understood. In this study, the conformational and functional behavior of recombinant hTK1 was systematically investigated using a combination of experimental and computational approaches. We observed that hTK1 retained its highest structural stability and catalytic activity at pH 8.0, exhibiting the greatest Vmax (1.363 +/- 0.06 muM s(-1)) and 100% relative activity. ANS fluorescence increased with lower pH, while ThT fluorescence, light scattering, and dynamic light scattering showed stronger signals associated with aggregation at higher pH. MD simulations and spectroscopic data showed that under extreme pH conditions, the structures were more flexible, hydrogen-bonding networks changed, solvent accessibility increased, and correlated residue motions were disrupted. The pH 8.0 condition was characterized by a single conformational cluster of hTK1, whereas the acidic and alkaline conditions were more conformationally heterogeneous. These structural perturbations substantially reduced kinase activity, strongly suggesting a relationship between protein conformation and kinase activity. The results show that the native conformation is crucial for maximal catalytic activity and provide molecular insights into hTK1 regulation under physiological and pathological conditions. We combine experimental characterization and MD simulations to probe the link between pH-dependent structural dynamics and hTK1 function, further strengthening hTK1's potential as a therapeutic target to cure diseases associated with altered nucleotide metabolism.

title: Evolutionary and dynamic constraints converge on a conserved coupling sector in thermally adapted GH1 beta-glucosidases.
authors: Zheng, Li-Ting; Li, Yi; He, Xian; Yang, Lian-Tao; Zhao, De-Rui; Liu, Meng-Ting; Sang, Peng; Yang, Li-Quan
abstract: How protein sequences evolve to maintain functional conformational dynamics under thermal stress remains an important question in molecular evolution. Thermophilic enzymes are often considered to achieve stability primarily through enhanced structural rigidity, yet thermal adaptation may also involve the preservation or reorganization of correlated motions across the protein scaffold. Here, we compared three glycoside hydrolase family 1 beta-glucosidases-BsBgl1A, 9UPT, and LQBG8-that share a conserved (beta/alpha)8 TIM-barrel fold but display distinct optimal temperatures of approximately 45, 65, and 70  degrees C, respectively. By integrating comparative structural analysis, three independent 1 mus molecular dynamics simulations at 300, 325, and 350 K, neural relational inference of residue-level dynamic coupling, and family-level coevolutionary analysis, we identified distinct dynamic strategies associated with their thermal phenotypes. All three enzymes retained their global compactness and principal secondary-structure framework across the simulated temperatures, indicating that differences in RMSD and residue flexibility did not reflect large-scale unfolding. BsBgl1A showed the strongest temperature sensitivity, with increased structural deviation and residue mobility at 350 K. Its inferred interaction network exhibited a non-monotonic response, characterized by pronounced overcoupling at 325 K followed by reduced connectivity at 350 K. In contrast, 9UPT maintained relatively restrained residue dynamics and a highly reproducible coupling topology across temperatures. LQBG8 combined substantial local conformational flexibility with persistent long-range coupling and retained the highest directed network density at 350 K. Across the three enzymes, the betaalpha5-betaalpha7 region repeatedly emerged as a shared structural and dynamic center. Coevolutionary couplings were also enriched in TIM-barrel-associated regions that spatially converged on this sector. These findings indicate that thermal adaptation in GH1 beta-glucosidases is not adequately explained by uniform structural rigidification. Instead, enzymes with the same conserved fold may adopt distinct organizations of correlated motion, while greater thermal adaptation is associated with the persistence or reorganization of a betaalpha5-betaalpha7-centered dynamic coupling pattern under elevated temperature. The correspondence between dynamic coupling and coevolutionary enrichment is consistent with long-term evolutionary constraint on this structural sector, although it does not establish direct selection on the network as an independent functional unit. Our results therefore provide a testable framework in which thermostability reflects a balance among local stabilization, regional flexibility, and the resilience of higher-order dynamic organization.

title: Structural basis for inhibition of the lipid flippase MurJ by phage lysis protein SglPP7 suggests convergent evolution with other Sgl peptides.
authors: Hosoda, Kaito; Kohga, Hidetaka; Wu, Sixian; Tanaka, Hiroyuki; Shigematsu, Hideki; Miyazaki, Ryoji; Chek, Min Fey; Tsukazaki, Tomoya
abstract: Some bacteriophages encode lysis proteins that inhibit essential bacterial processes, and elucidating their mechanisms is valuable for developing antibacterial strategies against drug-resistant pathogens. We determined the cryo-EM structure of the complex between the essential Escherichia coli lipid II flippase MurJ and the phage lysis protein SglPP7. Structural, mutational, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation analyses revealed that SglPP7 binds along the intramembrane cleft of MurJ and inserts its C-terminal tail into the internal cavity, stabilizing MurJ in an outward-facing conformation. Structural comparison with LysM (SglM) and SglCJ3 showed that these sequence-divergent Sgl proteins stabilize MurJ in the outward-facing conformation through distinct binding modes, consistent with the possibility of convergent evolution toward MurJ inhibition.

title: On the limits of marginal protein folding stability: methodological goals and drawbacks.
authors: Ferreiro, David; Zoni, Valeria; Arenas, Miguel
abstract: CONTEXT: Why do proteins remain at the edge of stability rather than evolving toward maximal thermodynamic robustness? Can we trust the computational methods that inform about when and how stability falls off that edge? Marginal stability, the confinement of protein folding free energies to a window of approximately 5-15 kcal/mol, is broadly observed in biophysics, and its mechanistic causes, involving evolutionary and biophysical properties, remain under debate and require accurate predictions. In this regard, protein folding stability is currently predicted using both traditional structure-based homology-modeling methods and modern sequence-based deep-learning methods. However, comparisons among these methodologies remain scarce. METHODS: Using four viral proteins of biomedical interest and considering that rapidly evolving viral proteins provide a useful system for understanding thermodynamic tolerance under the competing demands of structural integrity and adaptive flexibility, we compared predicted protein stability from both approaches across independent random mutational trajectories and naturally occurring sequence variants available in public databases. The results showed a general methodological impasse. As random mutations accumulated, structure-based methods predicted a progressive decline in stability toward collapse, a pattern driven by the enforced conservation of protein structure. In contrast, sequence-based methods failed as sequences moved into uncharted regions of parameter space. Together, protein stability landscapes predicted using current computational approaches are inherently shaped by technical limitations, leading to uncertainty in the evaluation of marginal stability and stability changes associated with biological processes.

title: Transformer Models in Vibrational Spectroscopy: A Review.
authors: Jafari, Jamile Mohammad; Bocklitz, Thomas
abstract: Transformer models have attracted increasing interest in vibrational spectroscopy because of their ability to capture long-range dependencies in spectral data. These models have been applied to analytical tasks including spectral preprocessing, classification, quantitative analysis, multimodal data fusion, and spectra-to-structure prediction. Their flexible architectures support applications in Raman, infrared (IR), near-infrared (NIR), and surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), with examples across chemistry, biology, and materials science. Transformer-based models also offer opportunities to integrate chemical, physical, and biological information in spectral analysis and support interdisciplinary research involving chemometrics, deep learning, and experimental spectroscopy. In this review, we elucidate the fundamental principles of Transformer models and their wide-ranging applications in vibrational spectroscopy, spanning from baseline correction and deconvolution to molecular identification, disease diagnosis, food authentication, and quantitative property prediction. Finally, as Transformer models may not be suitable for every analytical task or consistently outperform simpler approaches, we discuss current challenges and future trends in Transformer models in vibrational spectroscopy and related analytical sciences.

title: Comparative Conformational Sampling of Apo Adenylate Kinase by Enhanced Molecular Dynamics and a Sequence-Based Generative Ensemble Model.
authors: Zhao, Qingling; Cui, Ting; Li, Ying
abstract: Conformational sampling remains a major challenge in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of proteins with large-scale functional motions. Here, we use apo Escherichia coli adenylate kinase (AdK) as a benchmark for the open-closed transition and compare nine sampling protocols under a uniform explicit-solvent budget of 300 ns per method. The methods include unbiased MD, metadynamics, targeted MD (TMD), accelerated MD, simulated tempering, interpolation-based MD, and BioEmu. Closed-state sampling was evaluated relative to a reference-closed basin defined from ligand-stripped PDB 1AKE. TMD was the only method that both reached and maintained the closed reference, whereas unbiased MD did not enter this basin within 300 ns. Metadynamics increased sampling along the domain-distance coordinate but also promoted excessive LID opening, while simulated tempering showed a similar tendency. BioEmu generated closed-like conformations, but these states were not maintained during subsequent short MD simulations. Overall, the results show that collective-variable coverage does not necessarily correspond to stable target state occupancy and that different sampling methods provide different types of conformational information. These findings highlight the importance of selecting sampling strategies according to the specific scientific objective.

title: The Disordome Paradigm: How Intrinsic Disorder Encodes Emergent Biological Function.
authors: Fantini, Jacques; Lefebvre, Marine; Aulas, Anais; Chahinian, Henri; Yahi, Nouara
abstract: Classical structural biology equates function with a fixed three-dimensional fold, a view challenged by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and regions (IDRs), which populate broad conformational ensembles rather than a unique structure. This article introduces the "disordome" paradigm, extending Uversky's "unfoldome" to describe how function emerges from electrostatic and hydration landscapes that reshape reversibly upon encounter with a partner. Using alpha-synuclein binding to ganglioside-enriched rafts and IDR-driven liquid-liquid phase separation, we argue that transient folding-upon-binding events, potentially entropically cheap, generate information-rich complexes and condensates that dissolve once conditions change, consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. We trace this logic to overlooked precursors: in 1957 Klotz invoked rubber elasticity to introduce entropy as the driver of protein "disorientation", while in 1962 Bernal described such proteins as chains "coiled in different ways" and formulated a "two-atom rule" whereby bonding constraints fix atomic geometry only up to two atoms apart. We argue that the local under-determination described by this two-atom rule, left unresolved in IDPs by any conserved network of contacts, helps explain why AlphaFold fails on IDPs. A quantum-mechanical pillar (dispersion, OH-pi contacts, tunneling) is proposed as underrepresented in IDP research. We discuss implications for the origin of life, cellular regulation via condensates, and a therapeutic logic ("target the target, not the arrow") illustrated by AmyP53, which occupies raft gangliosides rather than disordered amyloid proteins in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

title: CRISPR/Cas12a-Based Aptasensor for Cas9 Protein Detection in Spiked Food Matrices.
authors: Wang, Zizhao; Wang, Jing; Li, Ling; Chen, Guofeng; Wen, Hongtao; Liu, Baohai; Dong, Yiyang
abstract: Residual gene editors are a concern associated with the widespread application of CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Here, we developed a CRISPR/Cas12a-based fluorescent aptasensor for the qualitative and quantitative detection of Cas9 protein. Secondary structure prediction and molecular docking were combined to identify potential binding sites of the Cas9-specific aptamer. A fluorescence aptasensor was constructed based on competitive binding: in the presence of Cas9, the aptamer binds to the target and releases complementary DNA (cDNA), which activates the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a. Cas12a subsequently cleaves a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporter labeled with a fluorophore and a quencher, generating a fluorescence signal, expressed in relative fluorescence units (RFU), that increases with Cas9 concentration. The optimized conditions comprised a trans-cleavage reaction time of 20 min, a Cas12a:CRISPR RNA (crRNA) molar ratio of 1:1, a final aptamer concentration of 180 nM, and a combination of low- and high-salt buffers to balance molecular recognition and protein stability. The proposed assay enabled Cas9 protein detection in buffer and Cas9-spiked soybean milk and cereal matrices. These results represent a proof-of-concept evaluation in complex food matrices rather than validation of authentic residual Cas9 detection. Further studies using unspiked gene-edited samples with independently verified Cas9 residues and an orthogonal reference method are required.

title: Navigating the Eukaryotic Paradox: Insights for AI-Driven Computational Strategies Against Antifungal Resistance.
authors: Tullio, Vivian
abstract: The escalating crisis of invasive fungal infections and increasing antifungal resistance demand rapid therapeutic innovation. Given the critically narrow clinical arsenal, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have emerged as pivotal strategies to accelerate drug repurposing, providing a rapid alternative to de novo drug discovery. However, translational success in medical mycology faces a major biological hurdle: the "eukaryotic paradox," the extensive genomic, metabolic, and structural homology between fungal cells and human hosts. This review provides a critical and comparative analysis of AI-driven drug repurposing as a therapeutic strategy. This review characterizes the hierarchies of structural barriers, biophysical transport bottlenecks, and computational failure modes across bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens to explain why medical mycology remains one of the most difficult frontiers in computational pharmacology. It reviews limitations of fungal cell walls, biofilm EPS matrices, morphologic dynamic dimorphism, and scarcity of high-resolution 3D protein structures for AI models. Next-generation computational approaches and experimental platforms, ranging from physics-informed neural networks and transcriptomic profiling to microfluidic organ-on-a-chip validation systems, are also described to overcome these resistance mechanisms. Finally, this review emphasizes the importance of the development of tailored, physics-informed AI paradigms for effective therapeutic strategies against emerging resistant fungal pathogens.

title: Type III Effectors of Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Manipulation Networks, and Implications for Plant Disease Resistance.
authors: Zhong, Xiaoju; Huang, Jianzhong
abstract: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst DC3000) is a reference system for dissecting how type III-secreted effectors (T3Es) suppress plant immunity and reconfigure host physiology. Here, we reassess the DC3000 effector repertoire through an evidence-graded framework that links experimentally resolved effector-target mechanisms to repertoire-level genetic interactions and, ultimately, to disease-resistance strategies. We distinguish findings demonstrated with Pst DC3000 from mechanistic examples derived from other P. syringae pathovars and from computationally generated hypotheses. At the molecular level, validated DC3000 effectors perturb pattern-recognition receptor signaling, protein turnover, vesicle trafficking, plasmodesmatal communication, organelle function, and hormone-associated processes. At the repertoire level, deletion and reconstruction studies reveal functional redundancy, specialization, conditional suppression, and context-dependent interactions; importantly, convergence on a common host phenotype is not treated as evidence of direct physical cooperation between effectors. We further evaluate how effectoromics, multi-omics, single-cell and spatial approaches, structure prediction, and machine-learning tools can prioritize new hypotheses while emphasizing their need for genetic, biochemical, and infection-based validation. Finally, we consider how conserved effector targets, susceptibility factors, NLR engineering, and CRISPR-based editing may translate mechanistic knowledge into more durable bacterial-disease resistance. This synthesis positions the DC3000 system as a bridge between mechanistic effector biology, quantitative effector-network analysis, and experimentally testable strategies for crop protection.

title: alpha-Halogenated Curcumins Enhance the Binding Affinity and Induced Structural Alterations to Amyloid-beta Protein in Alzheimer's Disease.
authors: Khan, Mateen A; Chinnappan, Raja; Andole, Sowmya; Akif, Mohd; Mir, Tanveer Ahmad; Yaqinuddin, Ahmed; Pham, Phuong-T T; Bader, Mamoun M
abstract: Amyloid-beta (Abeta) aggregation and associated structural changes are central features of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. In this study, we investigated the binding of alpha-halogenated curcumins, alpha-bromocurcumin and alpha-chlorocurcumin, to Abeta(1-42) and examined their effects on the peptide secondary structure using fluorescence spectroscopy and circular dichroism (CD). Both alpha-halogenated curcumins interacted with Abeta(1-42), but their binding properties differed from those of the parent curcumin. alpha-Chlorocurcumin exhibited a higher binding affinity for Abeta(1-42) than curcumin, whereas alpha-bromocurcumin showed comparatively weaker binding. Temperature-dependent binding studies revealed that the association of alpha-halogenated curcumins with Abeta(1-42) was influenced by temperature, with reduced binding affinity at higher temperatures. Thermodynamic analysis demonstrated favorable free-energy changes for the interactions and revealed that alpha-halogenation altered the relative enthalpic and entropic contributions to Abeta(1-42) binding. CD analysis further showed that binding of the curcumin altered the secondary structure of Abeta(1-42). These structural changes were more pronounced in the presence of the alpha-halogenated derivatives, indicating that halogen substitution influences the interaction and conformational response of Abeta(1-42). Molecular docking analysis provided additional insight into the possible binding modes and predicted intermolecular contacts between the alpha-halogenated curcumin and Abeta(1-42). Overall, the findings demonstrate that alpha-halogenation modulates the binding and structural effects of curcumin derivatives on Abeta(1-42), with alpha-chlorocurcumin exhibiting particularly favorable binding characteristics. These findings provide a basis for further investigation of alpha-halogenated curcumins as potential modulators of Abeta-related molecular processes associated with AD.

title: Irreversible Inhibition of Human Ornithine Aminotransferase: A Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics Study.
authors: Zhang, Yixin; Guan, Xu; Gong, Anbao; Wang, Guoqiang; Zhang, Qingzhu; Li, Yanwei; Wang, Wenxing; Wang, Qiao
abstract: Human ornithine aminotransferase (hOAT) is overexpressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and participates in glutamine anabolic metabolism, making it a promising therapeutic target. Although (1S,3S)-3-amino-4-(hexafluoropropan-2-ylidenyl)-cyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid (named here as BCF(3) after the (bis)trifluoromethyl feature) has been proposed as a potent inhibitor of hOAT, previous experimental studies have characterized an external aldimine intermediate and the static end-state adduct, but the elementary fluorine-elimination steps and their modulation by the active-site environment remain incompletely understood. Herein, molecular dynamics (MD) and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations were employed to systematically explore the irreversible inhibitory mechanism mediated by external aldimine II-the key reaction intermediate of BCF(3)-against hOAT. Conserved active-site water molecules act as proton-shuttling bridges, and residue-dependent electrostatic effects control fluorine elimination. External aldimine II forms a stable covalent adduct with Lys292 and sequentially releases fluorine atoms from the -CF(2) moiety via water-mediated F(alpha-) and F(beta-) elimination, with feasible barriers of 10.8 and 16.0 kcal/mol, respectively. Negative overall reaction energies indicate that the elimination products are energetically favored in the system. Electrostatic and noncovalent interaction analyses suggest that Arg180 and Gly42 promote fluorine elimination whereas Phe177 suppresses it, providing an atomistic explanation for the superior inhibitory potency of the bis-trifluoromethyl scaffold. The atomistic inhibitory mechanism uncovered in this study provides a theoretical foundation for the future rational design of hOAT-targeted drugs for hepatocellular carcinoma therapy.

title: Linear Combination Properties of Spectral Phasors Allow Thermodynamic Analysis of Reversible Denaturation of Multidomain and Membrane Proteins.
authors: Recoulat Angelini, Alvaro A; Malacrida, Leonel; Gonzalez Flecha, F Luis
abstract: Denaturation of small globular proteins is often described as a reversible two-state transition between native and denatured conformations. Conversely, multidomain and membrane proteins frequently populate several partially folded intermediate states during denaturation. Traditional thermodynamic analysis of fluorescence intensity often fails to reliably identify these intermediate states. Alternatively, spectral phasors provide an effective model-free way to monitor these complex conformational changes by resolving overlapping fluorescence signals with small differences in the position or shape of the spectra. Nevertheless, converting phasor trajectories into quantitative thermodynamic information remains challenging when quantum yields do not remain constant during a given process, thus limiting their application to protein stability studies. In this work, we introduce a thermodynamic framework for quantifying protein stability from phasor trajectories. We validate this formalism using simulated spectral data generated from two- and three-state transitions, including changes in fluorescence quantum yields, successfully recovering the thermodynamic parameters used to generate the simulations. Additionally, we applied this approach to analyze published data on urea-induced unfolding of E. coli Outer Membrane Protein A. Phasor analysis identified a two-state transition, and the thermodynamic parameters agreed well with those obtained from total fluorescence intensity, supporting the validity of the proposed approach. Finally, applying this framework to the SDS-induced denaturation of Archaeoglobus fulgidus Cu(I)-transport ATPase enabled a complete thermodynamic characterization of the three transitions identified by phasor analysis of intrinsic fluorescence, which could not be resolved using fluorescence intensity alone. This formalism establishes fluorescence spectral phasors as a powerful quantitative approach for protein stability analysis.

title: Actions of Pharmaceutical Lactones and Lactams on the Enzymes with Lactonase Activity: In Silico Prediction and In Vitro Study.
authors: Efremenko, Elena; Domnin, Maksim; Sarapina, Anastasia; Zagidulina, Aigul
abstract: Pharmaceutical pollutants that contain lactone or lactam rings in their structure are frequently detected in wastewater. Enzymes with lactonase activity, synthesized by the microorganisms in aerobic activated sludge, are expected to be able to participate in the hydrolysis of these pharmaceutical pollutants, but the actual activity of many lactonases towards such compounds remains poorly characterized. In this work, a systematic molecular docking study of 12 enzymes and 39 pharmaceutical pollutants (beta-lactam antibiotics, macrolides, coumarins, statins) was undertaken. The binding affinity, active-site occupancy, total enzyme surface occupancy and geometric characteristics of the molecules (the distance from the catalytic nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of the lactone ring, and the attack angle formed between the nucleophilic atom of the enzyme and the C-N/C-O bond of the substrate) were evaluated in silico for a set of hydrolases displaying lactonase activity (AidC, AaL, hexahistidine-tagged organophosphate hydrolase (His(6)-OPH), etc.) and metallo-beta-lactamases (MbetaLs) (NDM-1, MIM-1, SAM-1). Lactamases exhibited favorable intermolecular interaction geometry for the majority of beta-lactams. No enzyme was found that satisfied the geometric criteria corresponding to the biodegradation of macrolides. With coumarins, only Paraoxonase PON2 provided an optimal geometry of biocatalysis; however, this enzyme is absent from activated sludge but may be of interest for in vivo applications. For several statins widely used in practice, combinations with enzymes having virtually ideal geometry for biocatalysis were identified: AidC/rosuvastatin lactone, AaL/lovastatin, His(6)-OPH/mevastatin, and PON2/simvastatin. For the first time, several pharmaceutical lactones were identified in silico and confirmed in vitro as inhibitors of MbetaL and His(6)-OPH. Competitive inhibition of NDM-1 by lactone-containing signaling molecules of Gram-negative bacteria present in activated sludge was revealed for the first time both in silico and in vitro. The obtained results' may be taken into account when implementing monitoring of biological stages at water treatment stations and improve the efficiency of water purification. The revealed characteristics of MbetaL inhibition by macrolides may be taken into account as one of possible explanations for the effective application of beta-lactams in combinations with macrolides known from multiple paratactical investigations.

title: From Prediction to Generation: Artificial Intelligence Reconstructing the Paradigm of Protein Glycosylation Research.
authors: Zhu, Junhong; Huang, Shuang; Zhang, Nannan
abstract: Among post-translational modifications, protein glycosylation is distinguished by its abundance and structural intricacy. Unlike protein biosynthesis, glycan assembly follows no template; it reflects glycosyltransferase/glycosidase competition, sugar-donor availability, and organelle-enforced compartmentalization, yielding heterogeneous glycoforms that confer functional versatility but complicate analysis. Three bottlenecks persist: stereochemical control in chemical glycosylation, ambiguous assignment of occupancy sites, and reproducing native conformations of fully glycosylated proteins. Adopting the "glycan language" framework, we survey how AI addresses each, emphasizing the systems on which it has been tested. In synthesis planning, GlycoPredictor uncovered anomeric-selectivity rules such as the anti-nitrile and C2-azido alpha-directing effects, while Bayesian optimization discovered lithium-salt-directed stereoselective glycosylation; for site identification, ESM-2 with AlphaFold2-derived structural features improves N- and O-glycosite prediction, and DeepGlycanSite maps carbohydrate-binding interfaces. For structure and dynamics, AlphaFold3 and multimodal cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, and molecular dynamics (MD) modeling move glycoproteins toward conformational ensembles, as in the AI-assisted dissection of the MCTS1-JAK2-IFN-gamma axis. In glycomics, deep learning resolves intact glycopeptides and de novo glycan topology and has defined Fc N-glycan signatures of immunoglobulin G in autoimmune and malignant disease. Because glycan language models link sequence and structure to function, they are becoming clinically actionable: they prioritize candidate variants in congenital disorders of glycosylation and stratify immune disorders and tumors by aberrant glycosylation. Remaining obstacles include scarce structure-linked datasets, encoding of branched topologies, multimodal fusion, and interpretability.

title: Integrative Bioinformatics Analysis Incorporating Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Identifies Putative Pathogenic HNF1B Missense Variants Associated with HNF1B-MODY.
authors: Aldharee, Hitham
abstract: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5 (MODY5 or HNF1B-MODY) is a rare form of diabetes caused by variants in HNF1B. Patients with MODY5 exhibit high blood sugar levels and symptoms commonly associated with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes (T1D, T2D), along with kidney and pancreatic issues. Nonetheless, diagnosis, treatment and management approaches depend on specific genotype-phenotype associations. Interpretation of HNF1B missense variants remains challenging because of conflicting classifications and limited clinical evidence. This study aimed to improve the interpretation of HNF1B missense variants with conflicting evidence regarding pathogenicity and thereby advance the genetic and molecular understanding of HNF1B-MODY. An integrative computational approach combining artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and conventional bioinformatic tools, including Panther, SIFT, SNAP2, Meta-SNP, PhD-SNP, PolyPhen-2, and AlphaMissense, was used to identify deleterious missense variants in the HNF1B gene. The variants were further processed to determine their effects on protein conformation, stability, function, and conservation across species. Among 982 reported variants retrieved from the ClinVar database, 368 were classified as missense. Only 47 missense variants were labelled with conflicting classification and reported with clinical uncertainty. Consensus analysis by all tools identified five candidate variants (His153Arg, Asn298Asp, Arg303His, Lys305Glu, and Val458Gly), representing 10.6% (5/47) as potentially pathogenic. AlphaMissense classified all five as likely pathogenic, with scores ranging from 0.8921 to 1.000. Secondary structure analysis indicates that the His153Arg, Asn298Asp, Arg303His, and Lys305Glu variants are in the helical region, while the Val458Gly variant is located within the coil region. Interestingly, all five filtered variants are predicted by the I-Mutant and MuPro tools to reduce protein stability. The three-dimensional (3D) protein structures were constructed using the Deep Learning-Based Iterative Threading Assembly Refinement (D-I-TASSER) tool and visualised by UCSF Chimera. Structural modelling showed similarity between the mutant and wild-type models, with RMSD values ranging from 0.77 to 1.36 A. The multiple sequence alignments show that amino acids at variant sites across all variants are highly conserved among species. These findings show that combining traditional bioinformatics with artificial intelligence and machine learning improves the interpretation of HNF1B missense variants with clinical uncertainty. Integrating computational predictions with structural, evolutionary, and clinical data provides a framework for prioritising variants for further functional and clinical investigation.

title: Peptidomics and Computational Docking Prioritize Candidate Peptide-Protein Associations Relevant to Upper-Gastrointestinal Biology in a Fermented Soy-Derived Postbiotic.
authors: Tremblay, Annie; Harms, Chase; Nankar, Amit; Gupta, Ravi; Buko, Alex; Tompkins, Thomas A
abstract: Background/Objectives: Gastro-AD((R)) (GAD) is a fermented soy-derived postbiotic supported by clinical and preclinical evidence related to gastric comfort and mucosal injury. Although fermentation-derived metabolites have been characterized, the peptide fraction remains poorly defined. This study characterized GAD peptides and explored their potential biological contexts. Methods: Untargeted peptidomics was used to identify soy-derived peptides in GAD and map them to source proteins. A diversity-sampling panel of ten peptides was selected using sequence, physicochemical, and predicted structural features. These peptides were screened against a human protein-structure library by computational docking, followed by GO enrichment and context-based prioritization of candidate interactors. Results: A total of 219 peptides, originating predominantly from soybean storage proteins, were identified. The GAD peptide fraction contained extensive overlapping sequence families and truncation ladders, consistent with extensive proteolytic processing. Three literature-reported antioxidant peptide sequences were identified as exact contiguous regions within longer GAD peptides. Large-scale docking against the screened human protein-structure library combined with GO-enrichment recurrence analysis and an independent review of top-ranked docking-derived candidates identified 180 candidate protein targets spanning innate immune and inflammatory defense, protease activity and peptide processing, extracellular-matrix remodeling, tissue repair and wound healing, and apoptotic signaling and epithelial turnover. Repeated randomized-affinity controls yielded substantially fewer FDR-significant GO terms than the observed docking-derived rankings, supporting non-random functional structure in the docking-derived protein rankings without establishing the accuracy of individual peptide-protein interactions. Context-based prioritization identified 43 unique Tier 1 and Tier 2 candidates with direct or context-dependent extracellular accessibility. The prioritized biological contexts included mucosal immune regulation, extracellular-matrix remodeling, epithelial turnover, and tissue restitution. Conclusions: The GAD peptide fraction described herein comprises multiple overlapping peptide families whose prioritized biological contexts center on mucosal defense, remodeling, and tissue restitution. These findings support further investigation of peptides as potential contributors to the multi-component biological properties of GAD.

title: Structure-Function Relationships of Cid1 Poly(U) Polymerase: Catalysis, Substrate Recognition, Engineering, and Applications.
authors: Chen, Yang; Wang, Pengbo; Zhang, Chenglong; Liu, Quanyong; Goh, Kian Mau; Zhang, Shoutao
abstract: RNA 3'-end modification is an important regulatory mechanism that influences RNA processing, stability, localization, function, and degradation. Beyond its biological roles, RNA 3'-end modification has become a valuable tool in biotechnology, enabling applications in RNA labelling, sequencing, engineering and oligonucleotide synthesis. Terminal nucleotidyltransferases are key enzymes responsible for template-independent nucleotide addition to RNA molecules. Among these enzymes, Schizosaccharomyces pombe Cid1, a poly(U) polymerase, has emerged as an important model for understanding RNA-specific terminal nucleotidyltransferase activity. Structural and biochemical studies have revealed how nucleotide recognition, metal-ion-dependent catalysis, RNA positioning, and conformational dynamics regulate Cid1-mediated uridylation. Recent advances in protein engineering, molecular simulation, machine learning, and generative protein design have further expanded Cid1 functionality, generating variants with improved activity, altered substrate specificity, and potential applications in enzymatic RNA synthesis. This review summarizes the biological functions, structural characteristics, catalytic mechanisms, protein engineering strategies, and emerging biotechnological applications of Cid1, as well as the remaining challenges, highlighting its potential as a programmable platform for RNA 3'-end functionalization and enzymatic RNA oligonucleotide synthesis.

title: Salivary Proteomics Reveals Disease- and Therapy-Associated Molecular Patterns in Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis.
authors: Guadalupi, Giulia; Contini, Cristina; Piras, Chiara; Pisano, Giada; Frau, Jessica; Fenu, Giuseppe; Coghe, Giancarlo; Lai, Greca; Castagnola, Massimo; Messana, Irene; Diaz, Giacomo; Cabras, Tiziana; Olianas, Alessandra; Cocco, Eleonora; Manconi, Barbara; Lorefice, Lorena
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune-mediated disease for which non-invasive biomarkers, able to detect disease- and treatment-associated molecular changes, are needed. We characterized the whole-saliva proteome of patients with relapsing-remitting (RR) MS at baseline before treatment initiation (MS-T0; n = 66) and after six months of disease-modifying therapy (MS-T1; n = 40), in comparison with healthy controls (HC; n = 31). Nano-liquid chromatography-high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry identified 1305 proteins, of which 209 differed among the main comparisons. Pairwise and paired analyses distinguished persistent RRMS-associated alterations, baseline-attenuation patterns with changes shifting towards HC levels, treatment-associated differences emerging at MS-T1, and longitudinal-only alterations. The identified patterns are descriptive and cannot be interpreted as evidence of pharmacological treatment effects or clinical response. The existence of specific RRMS alterations was supported by exploratory Random Forest, which classified HC, MS-T0 and MS-T1 samples using a panel of 50 proteins, most of which (96%) also showed significant changes in univariate tests. Reactome enrichment evidenced that proteins pertaining to the identified patterns are mainly involved in innate immunity, neutrophil degranulation, cell-death pathways, cytokine signalling, and protein folding. These findings indicate that six months of therapy was associated with substantial salivary proteome changes and support saliva as a candidate biofluid for longitudinal molecular monitoring and non-invasive detection of treatment-associated salivary proteome variations in RRMS.

title: In Silico Structural Dynamics and Downstream Bioprocess of Recombinant Human SUMO-IL-33.
authors: Nguyen, Kim-Hung; Mai, Tan Thanh; Lam, Thua-Phong; Pham, Long-Hung Dinh; Do, Hoang-Han; Quach, Minh-Thanh; Thai, Khac-Minh; Le, Minh-Quan; Nguyen, Quoc-Thai
abstract: Interleukin-33 (IL-33) is a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases, yet inhibitor screening is hindered by high commercial protein costs. While expressing IL-33 as a SUMO fusion protein overcomes yield limitations in Escherichia coli, whether this intact chimera can directly serve as a screening surrogate remains unresolved. Here, we combined in silico simulations with empirical bioprocess optimization to establish a high-yield pipeline for native human IL-33 production. AI-based structure predictions (AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold) revealed distinct inter-domain dynamics mediated by a flexible linker. Molecular dynamics simulations of the compact RoseTTAFold model suggested potential steric occlusion near receptor-binding interfaces, whereas AlphaFold models exhibited extended conformations, highlighting model-dependent variations that warrant further structural verification. To restore accessibility, tag cleavage was optimized using 1.0% (mol/mol) SUMO protease at 4  degrees C for 1 h, achieving near-complete digestion. Sandwich ELISA demonstrated an 87.6% molar epitope recognition recovery for cleaved IL-33 versus only 12.0% for the intact fusion, providing empirical evidence of substantial functional epitope masking by the SUMO tag. Two-step IMAC purification yielded ~19% mass recovery (~32.6% molar recovery). These findings demonstrate that tag removal is operationally essential for IL-33 functional availability in screening applications.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Therapeutic Peptide Discovery and Development.
authors: Ventura, Salvador
abstract: Therapeutic peptides combine biological specificity with chemical versatility, and artificial intelligence (AI) now contributes to their identification, design, and optimisation. Peptide discovery, however, cannot be reduced to generating amino-acid sequences: therapeutic performance also depends on chemistry, conformation, assay context, stability, delivery, safety, manufacturability, and in vivo exposure. This critical review examines AI use across the major peptide classes: receptor agonists, protein-protein interaction inhibitors, oncology and tumour-targeting peptides, antimicrobial and phenotype-driven peptides, delivery peptides, vaccine epitopes, self-assembling materials, and chemically constrained macrocycles. It compares sequence-based, chemical, graph, structure-aware, and multimodal representations across predictive, generative, and experimentally integrated workflows. Coverage spans recent general protein foundation, prediction, and design systems (ProtGPT2, ESM-2/ESM3, ProGen/ProGen2, ProteinMPNN, RFdiffusion, and AlphaFold 3) and peptide-focused methods (RFpeptides, PepFlow, and PepGLAD). Particular attention is given to benchmark integrity, the limits of structure prediction for short and non-canonical molecules, and the gap between retrospective and prospective evidence. To make claims comparable, the review adapts established reporting, validation, and readiness concepts into a peptide-specific, two-dimensional Peptide-AI Evidence Grid that separates methodological rigour (M0-M3) from translational depth (T0-T3), applies it to representative studies, and provides a checklist extending DOME, TRIPOD + AI, and FAIR guidance with the chemistry- and assay-specific items peptide work requires.

title: Computational Studies of the Dynamics of the Human Iron Exporter Ferroportin and Insight into the Role of Crucial Residues Involved in Pathogenic Mutations.
authors: Vulterini, Sergio; Bonaccorsi di Patti, Maria Carmela; Musci, Giovanni; Polticelli, Fabio
abstract: Ferroportin (FPN/SLC40A1), the only known human iron exporter, plays a key role in iron homeostasis through an alternating access mechanism involving inward-open, occluded, and outward-open conformations. Pathogenic FPN mutations cause ferroportin-related iron overload, an autosomal dominant iron overload disease characterized by early-onset anemia, hepatic fibrosis, and diabetes. This disease can be further categorized into two subtypes: ferroportin disease, characterized by low transferrin saturation (TSAT) and iron overload predominantly in Kupffer cells, and ferroportin-related hemochromatosis, defined by high TSAT and iron overload in hepatocytes. However, the structural and functional characteristics governing FPN's conformational transitions and their relationship to pathogenic mutations remain poorly understood. Therefore, we conducted comprehensive modeling and molecular dynamics studies to investigate the conformational states of the transporter and analyze the molecular basis of disease-causing mutations. Our analysis revealed shared dynamic properties across FPN conformations, with all the three main conformations displaying stable protein cores surrounded by dynamic peripheral regions. We observed significant differences in the most stable interactions established between the two lobes of the transporter across the three conformational states, enabling identification of key residues involved in state-dependent stabilization. These findings were interpreted in the context of known pathogenic mutations to assess their potential effects on protein stability and transport mechanism. This approach provides crucial insights into the molecular determinants of FPN function and dysfunction, offering a foundation for understanding how specific mutations disrupt its specific conformational states and lead to ferroportin-related iron overload. The identification of conformationally important residues enhances our understanding of FPN's transport mechanism and provides a framework for interpreting the pathological consequences of genetic variants in iron metabolism disorders.

title: Microbial Rhodopsins: Structural-Functional Mechanisms and the Design of Optogenetic Silencing Tools-With Emphasis on Halorubrum Archaeorhodopsins.
authors: Chao, Luomeng; Yang, Yuxia
abstract: Microbial rhodopsins are light-sensitive membrane proteins that use retinal as a covalent chromophore and adopt a seven-transmembrane alpha-helical fold. They are widely distributed across archaea, bacteria, algae, and fungi and mediate diverse functions, including light-driven ion transport, light-gated ion conduction, and photosensory signaling. Since the discovery of bacteriorhodopsin in 1971, the microbial rhodopsin family has expanded continuously, and channelrhodopsin-based optogenetics has revolutionized neuroscience by enabling millisecond-scale optical control of neuronal activity. However, compared with excitatory tools, optogenetic silencing tools have developed more slowly and remain limited by insufficient photosensitivity, poor membrane localization, ion-homeostasis perturbation, and phototoxicity. Because these properties are largely constrained by the structural and functional features of the parent microbial proteins, the discovery and in-depth characterization of natural rhodopsins remain essential for tool innovation. This narrative review focuses on ion-pumping archaeorhodopsins, with emphasis on the genus Halorubrum and on HeAR, and describes how the literature was selected. We first summarize the functional classification, structural basis, photocycle, and ion-pumping mechanisms of microbial rhodopsins. We then discuss the diversity of Halorubrum archaeorhodopsins and the structural-functional features of HeAR, a recently characterized archaeorhodopsin from a halophilic archaeon isolated from Ejinoor Salt Lake in Inner Mongolia, China. HeAR absorbs at 550 nm (dark-adapted) and 560 nm (light-adapted), essentially the same maximum as AR3 (559 nm). Its Schiff-base counterion Asp-95 has a pKa of 3.5 +/- 0.1, about one unit higher than BR Asp-85 ( approximately 2.6) and AR3 Asp-95 (2.5 +/- 0.2), but matched by AR4 Asp-85 (3.6); thus, this is a property that HeAR shares with its closest relative rather than one that sets it apart. Its photocycle ( approximately 100 ms) is prolonged-roughly ten times longer than the overall cycle of BR (11 ms), of AR4 ( approximately 10 ms) and of the O-decay of AR3 (tau  approximately  14 ms)-while its M intermediate forms and decays faster than in BR; relative to AR3 and AR4, however, the M decay is slower (3.3 ms against  approximately 390 micros and 0.55/3 ms) and the overall cycle is longer. These are established in vitro properties of the heterologously expressed protein, and because a pump moves a fixed, small number of charges per photocycle, low-light performance remains a hypothesis to be tested rather than a demonstrated advantage. In this review "red-shifted" is used in one sense only: HeAR's 550-560 nm window lies  approximately 80-90 nm to the red of excitatory channelrhodopsins ( approximately 470 nm); relative to BR it is blue-shifted by  approximately 18 nm, and relative to AR3 the two absorption maxima coincide. We further review the evolution of optogenetic silencing tools, from inward chloride pumps and outward proton pumps to light-gated anion channels and potassium channels, and discuss structure-guided rational design strategies, including structure prediction, molecular dynamics simulation, directed evolution, and machine learning-assisted engineering. Finally, we outline current challenges and future opportunities in phototoxicity, deep-tissue light delivery, clinical translation and the exploitation of halophilic archaeal resources, and we specify which experiments are required before HeAR can be judged as a silencing tool. Clinically validated optogenetics is kept separate throughout from speculative applications of newly characterized archaeorhodopsins. This review aims to provide a comparative framework linking the structural-functional properties of natural rhodopsins to the rational design of next-generation optogenetic silencing tools.

title: RASSF2 Under the Computational Microscope: Prediction of Destabilizing Missense Variants.
authors: Al-Eitan, Laith Naser; Abusalem, Mohammad Tareq; Alghamdi, Mansour Abdullah
abstract: BACKGROUND: RASSF2 is a tumor suppressor gene involved in multiple cancers such as colorectal and lung cancer. Different studies have focused on promoter hypermethylation as the main inactivation pathway of this gene, which leads to cancer proliferation and metastasis. Here, using a comprehensive in silico pipeline, we investigate, for the first time, the impact of missense variants on protein structure, stability, and interactions. METHODS: Multitiered computational tools were used to predict the most likely pathogenic and destabilizing nsSNPs; the impact of coding mutations on different gene expression was analyzed, and the impact of nsSNPs on PPIs using mCSM-PPI2 and MutPred-PPI was analyzed using predicted AlphaFold protein complexes. RESULTS: Of 454 variants, 19 variants were consistently predicted to be likely pathogenic and destabilizing, 14 variants were in the RA domain, and two variants were in the SARAH domain. V193D, L235P, L247P, and Y275C were conserved and exhibited severe structural and molecular alterations. Also, Y275C was at the interface, and it was predicted to disrupt the RASSF2-MST2 complex. KRT23 and BCL2L14 were significantly downregulated in samples containing mutated RASSF2 in COAD and LUAD, respectively. STRING illustrates the Hippo signaling pathway as the main pathway involved in the network. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide promising candidates that can be important for future functional investigations. However, in vivo and in vitro experiments to validate our findings are necessary.

title: Advances and Challenges in mRNA Cancer Vaccines: Individualized Design and Delivery.
authors: Huang, Liyun; Tang, Yuting; Chen, Xiaobing; Wu, Zhen; Xiao, Junlan; Xiang, Qi; Tian, Huajian
abstract: Since the widespread use of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines, significant progress has also been made in mRNA cancer vaccines. Currently, mRNA cancer vaccines represent one of the most promising treatments for advanced tumors, with several candidates in clinical trials. Compared with traditional treatment methods, mRNA cancer vaccines have several advantages. However, several challenges of mRNA cancer vaccines remain, including the accurate and rapid identification of neoantigens and hotspot mutations that match different HLA types. To address these challenges, we review four key aspects of mRNA cancer vaccine development. These include neoantigen identification technologies, machine learning and AI prediction, mRNA sequence and structure design, and the development of LNP delivery systems. Additionally, we analyze the pipelines of leading companies in this field, providing insights into personalized mRNA cancer vaccines. This review also discusses future challenges and prospects, aiming to help guide this promising field toward the full realization of its potential.

title: AI-Assisted WES Variant Interpretation in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Narrative Review of Existing Tools.
authors: Treccarichi, Simone; Vinci, Mirella; Musumeci, Antonino; Galati Rando, Rosanna; Fallea, Antonio; Brancato, Desiree; Bruno, Francesca; Federico, Concetta; Saccone, Salvatore; Elia, Maurizio; Cali, Francesco
abstract: Background/Objectives: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by alterations in brain development and function, frequently associated with complex genetic architectures. The widespread implementation of next-generation sequencing, particularly whole-exome sequencing (WES), has substantially increased the identification of potentially disease-associated variants, shifting the major challenge from variant detection to their interpretation and prioritization. This review examines the emerging contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to WES variant interpretation in NDDs, with particular emphasis on AI-assisted variant prioritization and protein structural modelling. Methods: We reviewed conventional computational and emerging AI-driven approaches applicable to different stages of WES interpretation, including variant pathogenicity and functional-effect prediction, evolutionary conservation, splicing assessment, phenotype-informed prioritization, and protein structure prediction. Their methodological principles, applications, and major limitations were critically examined within the context of neurodevelopmental genomics. Results: AI and machine-learning approaches increasingly integrate genomic, phenotypic, functional, and structural information, supporting phenotype-aware candidate prioritization and molecular contextualization of selected variants. However, computational outputs are affected by model-specific limitations and should not be considered independent evidence of pathogenicity. Their added value depends primarily on the complementarity and biological relevance of the information provided, rather than on predictor concordance alone. Conclusions: This narrative review highlights that AI-assisted WES interpretation should prioritize complementary, mechanism-relevant evidence over computational concordance. AI-assisted tools should therefore be selected according to variant class and disease mechanism and integrated with independent clinical, genetic, and functional evidence.

title: Ultrasound-Synchronized In Situ Crystallization Locks Transient High-Activity Enzyme Conformations within Covalent Organic Frameworks.
authors: Zhou, Hongli; Chen, Shuang; Zhou, Haiyue; Han, Yuxuan; Xin, Ruobing; Wang, Tiantian; Cao, Yufei; Chen, Qiang
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Enzymes transiently access high-activity conformations with exposed cryptic sites and heightened substrate affinity, yet these states dissipate upon relaxation to the thermodynamic ground state once the activating perturbation is removed, leaving this catalytic potential largely inaccessible. Here we show that such fleeting conformations can be captured by synchronizing enzyme activation with host crystallization in a single sonochemical process, where ultrasound simultaneously drives enzymes into open conformations and promotes aqueous crystallization of covalent organic frameworks that grow around and lock the activated proteins before relaxation occurs. Using a library of six frameworks with systematically varied pore sizes and chemistries, we find that effective locking requires both tight steric confinement and abundant nonbonded interactions. The optimal framework increased the catalytic activity of horseradish peroxidase by 3.4-fold, primarily through a marked reduction in the Michaelis constant, while retaining >70% activity over 10 catalytic cycles. Molecular dynamics simulations identify the captured species as a globally reorganized open state defined by displacement of gating phenylalanine residues, while high-resolution 2D solid-state NMR analysis further elucidates the COF-enzyme interfacial interactions that stabilize this otherwise metastable conformation. Moreover, ex situ controls in which activation precedes encapsulation fail entirely, establishing that temporal synchrony between conformational opening and framework crystallization is mechanistically essential. Extending this strategy to laccase, cytochrome c, and lipase enhanced immobilized enzyme activity by 3.8-fold, 2.7-fold, and 1.5-fold over conventional stirring. This work reframes enzyme immobilization from passive protection to active conformational upgrading, enabling a general strategy to harvest transient functional states beyond equilibrium reach.

title: Discovery and Mechanistic Investigation of a Bacteria-Derived Sesquiterpene Ether Synthase AceS Catalyzing Syn-Protoetherification.
authors: Liu, Yuanning; Zhang, Shouqi; Zou, Jiasheng; Xu, Wenqiang; Wang, Tao; Wang, Chen; Kong, Yao; Zhang, Pengcheng; Wang, Kaibiao; Hsiao, Po-Yun; Jia, Hongli; Liu, Fen; Yin, Min; Chang, Chin-Yuan; Xu, Zhengren
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: To discharge the carbocation in the termination step of terpene synthase (TS)-catalyzed cyclization, in addition to proton elimination to form alkene products and water quenching to afford hydroxylated products, intramolecular hydroxy group-trapping to give terpene ethers represents a variation of the latter case. Among the limited known TSs that are able to directly convert the linear oligoprenyl diphosphates to terpene ethers, 1,8-cineole synthase is the only characterized enzyme that catalyzes syn-protoetherification of the double bond in the termination step. We herein report the discovery and mechanistic investigation of a bacteria-derived sesquiterpene synthase AceS, converting farnesyl diphosphate to acorenol ether (1) in a syn-protoetherification manner. The unique 5/6 spiro-fused acorane skeleton with an ether ring bridging C3 and C7 of 1 was elucidated based on NMR analysis and X-ray diffraction (XRD) of a cytochrome P450-modified derivative. Labeling experiments using our recently developed "deuterium-scanning" approach allowed us to characterize a 1,2-hydride shift from C10 to C11 and a hydride shift from C6 to C10, as well as the syn-stereochemistry of the protoetherification process during cyclization. Results obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations, protein structure-guided site-directed mutagenesis, isolation and structural characterization of the products generated by the mutants, and protein-ligand docking simulations suggested cyclization through bisabolyl-dunnienyl cations as the favored pathway, albeit the coexistence of a pathway through carotenyl cations is also possible. Y186 may play as a key residue to redirect water to trap the C7 carbocation and to promote the syn-protoetherification reaction.

title: Recognition Loop Dynamics Differentiates m6A-mRNA Reader Domains of YTHDF Proteins.
authors: Li, Yaozong; Bedi, Rajiv Kumar; Ojeda-May, Pedro; Caflisch, Amedeo
journal: Journal of chemical theory and computation
abstract: The three human YTH-domain family proteins (YTHDF1, YTHDF2, and YTHDF3) are highly homologous and recognize the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of mRNA with essentially identical binding modes and affinities. This homogeneity challenges the well-established view that different YTHDF proteins play distinct cellular functions (the specificity view), with an emerging argument that these proteins may instead play redundant roles. To study this apparent discrepancy, we investigated the mechanism of binding of m6A-containing RNA using mutagenesis, X-ray crystallography, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), and molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, we compared different properties of YTHDF proteins, including their binding capacities to m6A-RNA, conformational changes, and homodimerization propensity. Our results show that the YTHDF proteins share an identical binding mode of m6A-RNA, which requires rare protonation of m6A for binding. Additionally, the three proteins share a similar open-closed switch for their recognition loop regulating the m6A binding. On the other hand, ITC data and crystal structures provide consistent evidence that the YTHDF proteins differ significantly in the flexibility of the recognition loop and its conformational preferences. Only YTHDF1 can homodimerize, which prevents binding to m6A-RNA. Furthermore, we integrate the available biophysical and biochemical evidence to define both the shared and distinct features of YTHDF1-3 in m6A-RNA recognition and propose a hybrid model that reconciles the redundancy-specificity debate. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the work and propose experiments for validating the presented model.

title: Predictive beta-Sheet Protein Stabilization via Computationally Guided Metal Coordination with Simulations and AlphaFold3.
authors: Lu, Zhuojian; Xu, Shengbang; Zheng, Bin; Wan, Aoqi; Wang, Ruishi; Tian, Yifeng; Liu, Hongjia; Wang, Yanwei; Zheng, Peng
abstract: Proteins that withstand mechanical forces in nature possess evolved architectures that resist forced unfolding, yet mimicking this robustness in engineered proteins remains challenging. Although metal coordination bonds can act as powerful molecular clamps, their incorporation has been largely empirical, with no rational method to identify where reinforcement would be most effective. Here, we present a predictive workflow that integrates all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to identify mechanical soft spots, AlphaFold3 (AF3) to assess the structural feasibility of engineered metal-chelating sites, and single-molecule force spectroscopy for experimental validation. Applying this approach to two previously AI-designed mechanostable beta-sheet proteins from the SuperMyo series, we demonstrate that Ni2+ coordination produces site-dependent reinforcement, with single-site variants producing substantial increases in unfolding force. Combining multiple coordination sites produced cumulative reinforcement, with a triple-site variant achieving a >110% gain and an unfolding force exceeding 400 pN. This closed-loop strategy connects computational prediction with experimental validation for the reinforcement of protein mechanical stability. Through programmable, site-specific metal coordination, the workflow enables systematic tuning of mechanical properties in beta-sheet protein scaffolds.

title: Divergent Catalytic Strategies of Group-6 Propane Monooxygenases in Propane-Stimulated 1,4-Dioxane Biodegradation.
authors: Yang, Junwon; Dhakal Gaudel, Devi Kumari; Antunes, Jose Manuel Diaz; Zheng, Wenwei; Li, Mengyan
abstract: Group-6 propane monooxygenases (PRMs) catalyze the initial oxidation of 1,4-dioxane (dioxane), a widespread contaminant of emerging concern. Because their expression can be induced by propane, an inexpensive and readily deliverable substrate, PRM-containing microorganisms offer a distinct advantage for propane-based biostimulation strategies targeting dioxane removal. However, functional differences among PRMs from the three major phylogenetic clusters remain poorly understood. Here, three PRMs from Mycobacterium dioxanotrophicus PH-06, Mycobacterium marinum E11, and Mycobacterium sp. ENV421, representing phylogenetic clusters, PRM-I, PRM-II, and PRM-III, respectively, were heterologously expressed in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc2155. ENV421 PRM-III exhibited low substrate affinity but high catalytic capacity toward both dioxane and propane, and moderate resistance to chlorinated solvent inhibition. In contrast, E11 PRM-II displayed high affinity but lower capacity and greater inhibitor sensitivity. PH-06 PRM-I showed comparatively stronger activity toward dioxane than propane relative to the other PRMs. Protein structure analysis suggested that variation in substrate affinity and catalytic turnover is consistent with differences in active-site pocket hydrophobicity, rigidity, and catalytic geometry.
