However, this does not prevent multiple models from collapsing onto the same high-reward areas, leaving large regions of the state space unexplored. With this in mind, we propose Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets (HCG), an approach that dynamically partitions the search space to coordinate discovery without relying on hand-crafted boundaries. HCG imposes an ordering in which the highest-ranked model may explore the entire space, while lower-ranked models are progressively pushed toward regions not covered by higher-ranked ones. We provide a theoretical characterization of how specific learning objectives can shift probability mass away from designated areas, instantiating this mechanism within our architecture. A shared classifier coordinates the hierarchy by partitioning the search space, keeping the GFlowNets independently parameterized and enabling asynchronous training. Furthermore, we derive a normalizer-weighted aggregation rule for the ensemble and prove that it recovers the target reward-proportional distribution under the stated assumptions. Finally, experiments across multimodal distributions, sequence generation, combinatorial optimization, and biological sequence design show that HCG improves mode coverage and target approximation, translating increases in the number of coordinated samplers into broader, complementary exploration.

title: Foldability Is an Intrinsic Property of Protein Sequences: A Lattice Model Study with Information-Theoretic Approach and Unsupervised Machine Learning
authors: Shubin Liu
abstract: Protein structure prediction has been largely solved, but why a given sequence is foldable has not. We address this question for 27-, 48- and 64-residue lattice heteropolymers with statistical thermodynamics, the informationtheoretic approach (ITA) and a variational autoencoder (VAE). Native populations, folding probabilities and freeenergy surfaces are reproducible and independent of the initial denatured ensemble, so foldability is an intrinsic property of the sequence at a given temperature and solvent. We then ask where the observed regularities come from. Stability is governed by an information balance: the information content (self-information) of the native energy relative to the maximum-entropy description of compact alternatives, ℐtail, must exceed their Shannon entropy, 𝑆c = ln𝛺c. This is the random-energy-model condition for a folding transition, and ℐtail/𝑆c fixes the ratio of folding to glass temperatures, recasting minimal frustration in information units. Foldable sequences have smooth funnels, minimal Shannon entropy and minimal Fisher information in the native state, and a single sharp maximum of Fisher information at melting (cooperativity). Mutual and conditional information show that stability is an approximately sufficient statistic for kinetic accessibility of compact 27-mers. No hierarchical folding order is found. Variational autoencoders trained without labels distinguish sequences by their folding ensembles, supply a six-variable reaction coordinate that retains 91% of the kinetic information in the full native-contact map, and rediscover the native energy gap from the density of compact states.

title: Borrowing the fold, building the site: non-catalytic protein scaffolds in the age of computational metalloenzyme design
authors: Andrea Rodil; Jan Deska
abstract: The design of novel metalloenzymes has gained its motivation and momentum less from what enzymes already do well rather than from what they do not do at all, that is, the organic chemistry outside any biosynthetic pathways. In search for starting points to create proteins that are active in new-to-Nature transformations, computational design in particular offers powerful solutions by supplying folds made to order en route to inventing tailor-made de novo biocatalysts. Nature, however, rarely invents; it decorates. A large share of biological catalysis sits on backbones whose original role was structural or recognition-based, and in which the metal center occupies no more than a handful of side chains within an otherwise unchanged fold. In this Perspective we make the case that especially in systems addressing abiological catalysis, promising and successful approaches oftentimes adapt non-catalytic scaffolds as their foundation, taking binding modules, small disulfide-locked domains and synthetic miniproteins as hosts. We organize the discussion around the minimal functional site: the smallest ligand set that, placed on a rigid and pre-organized backbone, holds a metal in a defined geometry. Whether a given scaffold is able to offer such a site is a structural question before it is a chemical one. We examine how far current structure prediction can guide the placement of such sites, where its confidence scores mislead, and which spectroscopic and computational evidence remains indispensable. Scaffold repurposing, we conclude, offers organic synthesis a route to catalysts that enzymology alone would not deliver.
